User-facing changes in each release, newest first. Each release has a
short summary; expand it for the itemised entries, where breaking changes
come first. Each release's GitHub page lists every merged pull request.
0.title: Changelog

2.text: A request held across the policy's valid_until, by an addon or while its body is buffered for inspection, is denied _expired when it reaches the rules, as a request sent after the instant is (#568).Without forwarded_for, client.ip is the canonical TCP peer address: an IPv4 client on a dual-stack [::] listener is a.b.c.d, not ::ffff:a.b.c.d, in metric keys, the flow log and the addon principal. Rule comparisons already treated the two as one address. client.peer.ip in the flow log keeps the socket's form (#579).JSON the node cannot parse, whether the node.token record, an enrolment or renewal response, a lease or a flow upload's acknowledgement, is reported by the kind of fault and its line and column, never by quoting the input, which could put a token or a lease secret in the log (#532).
2.title: Fixed

3.text: Addons can now answer early and hold a request or response for approval, with the request and response lanes of an exchange living independent lives. This is a breaking change for addons: the service protocol is roxy.layer.v6 and the WASM interface is roxy:addon@0.3.0. Details

4.text: The service layer protocol is roxy.layer.v6. It is incompatible with roxy.layer.v5 and the experimental roxy.layer.v0, and roxy does not accept a v5 peer: both sides must handle stop, trailers, explicit ends in both directions and headless completion. The bundled Python helper implements the new contract (#558).The WASM addon interface is roxy:addon@0.3.0. Components built against 0.2.x or the unversioned package must be rebuilt with the matching SDK and WIT (#558).
4.title: Breaking

5.text: An addon can answer before forwarding, hold a request or an upstream response while it decides, and stream approved content into an answer it has already started. An approval addon can send 200 text/event-stream with keepalive comments while it holds a request or a tool-call event, then approve, edit or deny it (#558).The request and response lanes of an exchange have independent lifetimes: a layer can end or stop one without the other, and an upstream head that arrives after an early answer is still delivered to the addon (#558).Trailers pass through service layers and WASM host-side passthrough, so gRPC status trailers survive an addon stack. WASM byte-stream rewriting has no trailer API and the Python forwarding helpers do not send trailers (#558).
5.title: Added

6.text: Upstream informational responses such as 103 Early Hints are discarded, with or without addons, and an addon cannot publish an informational head (#558).A WebSocket upgrade reserves its relay resources before the 101 reaches the client (#558).Publishing a second outgoing head on a lane is a layer failure and cuts an answer already in progress (#558).A layer that fails while handling a core denial may produce a 503, but the flow record keeps the original deny rule and reason; the layer fault gets its own event (#558).The final flow record for an exchange waits for both lanes' bodies, their validation and every accepted host call to finish (#558).The quickstart's sentinel sidecar streams a model response to the agent as it arrives, holding only each tool call's block while the sentinel judges it, instead of the whole response until the stream ends. A rejected call is replaced by its note in place, and modify now works on streamed responses (#563).A body that streams through a layer costs more CPU per byte than it did; the fixed cost of a layer is unchanged. Tracked in #561.
6.title: Changed

8.text: Quarantine, a bearer-token node protocol, host services for service layers and X-Forwarded-For support, plus two security fixes (GHSA-4297-w88p-8xqv, GHSA-pwq9-p79h-pg35). Breaking for control planes, service layers (roxy.layer.v5), client.port users and the per-addon state store. Details

9.text: Node protocol: a node's credential is a rotating bearer token instead of a client certificate. Enrolment returns token, not_after and renew_after_seconds; later requests send Authorization: Bearer; the state dir holds node.token in place of node.crt and node.key. A control plane built for mutual TLS no longer works (#528).The service layer protocol is roxy.layer.v5: the open message carries the layer's grants and config, and a service may send host-service calls on its stream (#526).client.port is removed as a rule field and metric key. The flow log keeps the TCP peer as client.peer: { ip, port }, so client.port moves to client.peer.port in the log (#525).The per-addon state store and the addons[].state block are gone: a WASM layer's state-get and state-put use the store the rules read with state[..], sized by limits.max_state_entries. A state-put without a TTL gets one hour, not six (#511).Stricter YAML: yes, no, on and off are not booleans, << merge keys and custom tags are errors, and a file holds one document (#482).
9.title: Breaking

10.text: Quarantine: a rule's quarantine action or a listener's quarantine_on.parse_errors threshold puts the proxy into a durable state where every exchange is refused 403 _quarantined. The trip is written to <state-dir>/quarantine and survives a restart; an operator removes the marker, or in node mode the control plane names the incident in the lease's quarantine.release list. roxy run --config accepts --state-dir, required when the config uses quarantine (#505).A layer of either kind can quarantine the proxy through the new quarantine capability: flow.quarantine for WASM, a quarantine message for a service (#529).Service layers get the host services WASM layers have: log, record, add_tag, state_get, state_put and metric_get messages, each answered with a result; capabilities and config are accepted on a service layer (#526).An http listener takes forwarded_for: { trusted_hops: N } to recover the client IP from X-Forwarded-For; the result is client.ip everywhere. A header with too few entries or a malformed trusted entry is refused 400 forwarded_for_invalid. The setting is a config error on an http_proxy listener (#525).Node protocol: the lease poll reports seq_unreserved when the node could not persist its flow sequence counter (#502).The docs site publishes each release under /vX.Y/ with a version menu (#522).
10.title: Added

11.text: The rule language calls a field admission when it is known at the forwarding decision and in-flight when it is re-checked as the exchange streams, in place of "head" and "watched"; roxy check, rule test and the compiler diagnostics use the new words (#524).A tag an enforce layer adds is visible to tag[..] in admission and in-flight rules and to the when of the layers below; the 64-tag / 4 KiB cap now counts the rules' tags too (#534).The wait for a busy layer instance is bounded by the layer's first_byte_timeout; past it the exchange fails closed with layer_error kind no_instance (#513).The health and CA listener has its own connection cap, so a client filling limits.max_connections on the proxy port cannot starve /healthz (#503).roxy check warns about a metric keyed on host or client.port without a where, with field-specific advice, and no longer warns for unique(..) fields (#497).The WIT package is roxy:addon@0.2.1, an additive bump that 0.2.0 components still load. The SDK's flow::metric_get loses its key parameter (#542).Node mode: a 401 on /renew is retried with backoff rather than ending renewal; 410 or 426 at enrolment is reported as a refusal (#546).A service observe stream ends on the service's last message rather than roxy's, with first_byte_timeout to send it, so a service observer can read a body and then record. Host calls queued before a stream ends still run (#548).A layer's own body that is still open splices the bypassed body as unknown length, so a held-back end or a failure is always a visible cut. A head-only WASM request layer that passes a stream to next now sends a chunked request upstream (#543).The node reserves flow sequence numbers off the emit path, so a slow disk no longer stalls every emitter (#485).
11.title: Changed

12.text: A WebSocket through a layer subscribed to (request: full, response: head) no longer stalls (#516).A service-layer head with too many header fields is refused at limits.max_headers instead of panicking (#499).Client parse-error detail is redacted in the operational log as it is in the flow log (#498).
12.title: Fixed

13.text: GHSA-4297-w88p-8xqv: Host: [::ffff:1.2.3.4] bypassed a deny on 1.2.3.4. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal now parses as the IPv4 address it embeds, and a host or tls.sni literal written in the mapped form is a compile error (#506).GHSA-pwq9-p79h-pg35: with http.allow_obs_text: true, a header value holding a byte of 0x80 or above was invisible to an equality rule but forwarded. Rules now read header values as the bytes that are forwarded, one character per byte (#507).YAML is read with serde-saphyr; the unmaintained unsafe-libyaml (RUSTSEC-2024-0449) is gone (#482). ruzstd 0.9.1 for RUSTSEC-2026-0344 (#505).
13.title: Security

14.text: Heads cross the WASM boundary as records and bodies as bare streams (roxy:addon@0.2.0), layers subscribe to only the directions they need, and a batch of host hardening fixes. Breaking for WASM components and service layers (roxy.layer.v4). Details

15.text: The WASM addon interface is roxy:addon@0.2.0: a head crosses the guest boundary as one record per direction and bodies are bare wasi:io streams; the wasi:http import is gone. Components must be rebuilt against SDK 0.2.0, which is source-compatible (#424).The service layer protocol is roxy.layer.v4: the deny message is gone (a service refuses by answering with a response) and open carries the layer's subscription (#420).Removed audit_endpoint, the audit flag of flow.record, endpoint retries and the attempts field of the endpoint_call event (#420).Removed the dead transparent-listener keys (mode: transparent, allow_passthrough, upstream_target); they are now unknown-field errors (#457).A host or tls.sni literal that can never match (trailing dot, non-ASCII, bracketed IPv6) is a compile error with a rewrite hint (#463).
15.title: Breaking

16.text: A layer declares what it wants of each direction with subscribe: { request: head | full, response: head | full }. A body a layer is not subscribed to bypasses it; bytes it passes on for that body fail the exchange closed (#420).SECURITY.md, pointing at private vulnerability reporting (#464).
16.title: Added

17.text: first_byte_timeout is one budget per head, request and response alike, for WASM layers as it already was for service layers (#431).Service layer streams spread across up to max_connections connections instead of filling one, and writes are flushed in batches (#423).The addon SDK moves bodies and heads a layer does not touch host-side, cutting a no-op layer's cost (#418).A fault after the response head carries its own reason into the request event (buffer_budget_exhausted, upstream_body_failed, layer_error or the client's parse reason) instead of response_write_failed (#419).like patterns are capped at 1 KiB and compiled with the same limits as matches; ? matches one character, as documented (#459).
17.title: Changed

18.text: A guest head with tens of thousands of header fields is refused at limits.max_headers instead of panicking the host (#458).A guest that writes to stdout or stderr no longer fails every exchange through its layer (#469).A handler that returns without responding is treated like a trap: the instance is discarded and the exchange fails (#460).An endpoint call waits for its in-flight permit before its body leaves the guest (#465).A service connection whose write side has died fails its exchanges at once with service:closed instead of after first_byte_timeout (#461).Body frames on an ended service stream are dropped without crediting, so a misbehaving service cannot grow roxy's memory (#462).response_body_idle_timeout applies while a response body is collected for inspection; a stalled upstream under a body rule gets a 504 (#467).The reference says what the code does where it overclaimed: timeouts, drain and linger limits, the hop-by-hop list, node 410 handling and lease fields (#457); HTTP/1.0 close-delimited responses are documented (#466).
18.title: Fixed

19.text: The first release: a strict, programmable HTTP firewall. Two ways to deploy it: as an egress proxy for a workload you don't trust (mode: http_proxy, with TLS terminated by roxy's own CA), or as a gateway in front of the APIs your clients call (mode: http).One canonical form: every request is parsed into one strict model and re-serialised, over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, with WebSockets relayed. Anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is denied.A typed YAML rule language where deny always wins and nothing unlisted passes; rules can watch bodies and WebSocket messages as they stream. Metrics give rate limits and byte budgets; secret injection and AWS SigV4 signing mean clients hold only placeholders.Addons above the rules, as WASM components in process or external services streamed over WebSocket: they can rewrite, withhold, answer or block, and the rules judge whatever they pass on.A JSONL flow log naming the rule or addon behind every decision, with optional body capture and digests; backpressure holds traffic until the log catches up.Node mode: roxy enrols with a control plane, leases its policy and secrets into memory, and ships its flow log.

20.text: roxy is a strict, programmable HTTP firewall. Every request and response streams through a pipeline you compose: addons that can rewrite, withhold, answer or block, then rules that judge exactly what they pass on. Run it as an egress proxy for a workload you don't trust, or as a gateway in front of the APIs your clients call. Every exchange takes the same path: roxy parses it, the addons see it, the rules judge it, and the connector dials the upstream (how roxy works). It fails closed: anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is denied.
20.title: Overview

21.text: Sandbox containment. An untrusted workload has no route out except through roxy. It points HTTPS_PROXY at roxy's proxy port and trusts roxy's CA; roxy decrypts each request, judges it, injects the credentials the workload never sees, and logs every decision. The network does the containing; roxy decides what gets out (sandbox containment). HTTP gateway. Clients address roxy directly, as anthropic.gw.example.com behind a load balancer that terminates TLS. Rules route each request by host and inject the real API keys, so clients hold placeholders; client authentication is an addon. It governs the traffic sent to it; it is not containment (HTTP gateway).
21.title: Use cases

22.text: The quickstart sends generated traffic through roxy with an auth gate, a per-user token quota and an inspect_sentinel sidecar, with roxy in node mode leasing its policy from a minimal control plane. Nothing in it needs an API key. examples/human-approval puts a person in the loop instead: Claude Code behind roxy, with every tool call held at the proxy until someone clicks Approve or Deny in the browser.

24.title: Open source

25.text: Run clients through roxy with three controls on every model call: a WASM addon that authenticates the client against an auth service, a WASM addon that holds each user to a token quota kept by a quota service, and an inspect_sentinel sidecar that blocks tool calls matching a denylist. roxy runs in node mode, leasing its policy and the model's API key from a minimal control plane and shipping its flow log back. The model is scripted and the traffic generated, so nothing needs an API key or a route out. The setup is examples/quickstart.
25.title: Quickstart

28.text: docker compose up --build --attach traffic The first run builds the images, which takes a few minutes. Eight containers start; only the last one's output is shown (Ctrl-C stops them): controlplane: enrols roxy, serves roxy.yaml and the model's API key as a one-minute lease, and prints the flow events roxy ships.roxy: the proxy on 127.0.0.1:3128, with the two addons at /etc/roxy/addons/. It has no config file; it runs the policy it leases.fake-model: answers POST /v1/messages from responses.json, one entry per call in order, streamed or whole, with the usage the real API sends. It refuses a request without the API key, which only roxy has.auth-service: alice-secret is alice and bob-secret is bob.quota-board: the quota service. Each user has a bucket of 600 tokens that refills at five a second.sentinel: the inspect_sentinel sidecar, on a network with no route out.inspect-view: Inspect's log viewer.traffic: the clients. Alice calls every six seconds, bob every twenty, and mallory, whose credential is unknown, every thirty.
28.title: Start the stack

29.text: Each client is the Anthropic SDK, pointed at the model through roxy, with its credential in an x-roxy-auth header; each call is one streamed POST /v1/messages. The scripted responses go by: a greeting, a Bash tool call running ls -la, then one running curl, which comes back as traffic-1  | [alice #2] I will fetch that page for you. roxy's sentinel blocked a Bash tool call (denylist match: 'curl'). The response streams to the client as the model produces it, except its tool calls: the sentinel holds each one from the start of its block to the end, judges it as soon as its arguments are complete, and then lets it through, rewrites its arguments or, as here, drops it and puts a note in its place. Text before and after a tool call streams live; events behind a held call wait their turn, with a ping every ten seconds while they do. When every tool call in a response is dropped, its stop_reason becomes end_turn, so the agent's turn ends as if the model had answered in words. Mallory is refused by the auth gate: traffic-1  | [mallory #1] 401 AuthenticationError: credential refused by the auth service Within the first minute alice drains her bucket, and her calls stop reaching the model until it refills: traffic-1  | [alice #8] 429 RateLimitError: token bucket empty (600 tokens, refills 5/s); try again in 15s
29.title: Watch the traffic

30.text:
Open http://127.0.0.1: each user's bucket, live, with the last five minutes of levels. The quota is per user, and the user is whoever the auth gate said. To make a call of your own: docker compose run --rm client --user bob
docker compose run --rm client --user mallory --secret wrong
30.title: Watch the quota board

31.text: Open http://127.0.0.1. Each client is a sample, grouped by the X-Claude-Code-Session-Id header it sends; its transcript shows every model call, the tool calls, and the sentinel's verdict under each: Continued, or Rejected with the reason. Reload the page to see new calls.
31.title: Watch it in Inspect View

32.text: docker compose logs roxy One line per request: the rule it matched, the addons it went through in order ("addons":["auth-gate","token-quota","sentinel"]), the user:alice tag the auth gate set, and the set_header:x-api-key mutation the rule made. The addons' own events are there too: endpoint_call for every call to the auth service and the quota board, layer_record for the verdicts and usage reports. Capture keeps whole requests and responses as well. The same events reach the control plane in batches, within the lease's five-second flush interval; docker compose logs controlplane shows each one prefixed with the node's id.
32.title: Read roxy's flow log

33.text: The lease is valid for sixty seconds and refreshed every fifteen. Stop the control plane: docker compose stop controlplane Within a minute every call fails with a 403 and roxy's /readyz answers 503 policy_expired: an unreachable control plane is not a reason to deny, but an expired lease is. docker compose start controlplane brings the next lease and roxy recovers without a restart. To revoke the node instead, add its id (the enrolled node-... line in the control plane's log) to the control plane's revoked file; the next poll answers 410 and roxy denies everything until it is re-enrolled: docker compose exec controlplane sh -c 'echo node-xxxxxx >> /data/revoked'
33.title: Let the lease run down

34.text: Ctrl-C in the terminal running up, then: docker compose down -v
34.title: Clean up

35.text: An exchange passes through the addons in the order roxy.yaml lists them, then the rules; each addon wraps everything below it. The auth gate (addons/auth-gate) reads the credential from x-roxy-auth, asks the auth service who it belongs to through a named endpoint, caches the answer in its state store under a hash of the credential, tags the flow user:alice, strips the header and passes the request on. A missing or refused credential is answered 401 and never leaves. The tag is how a layer hands an identity to the layers below; the rule injects the API key from a secret.The token quota (addons/token-quota) asks the quota board, before a model call leaves, whether the user's bucket holds anything (the user is the user: tag, or the client IP without one) and answers 429 with retry-after if not. Otherwise it reads input_tokens from message_start and output_tokens from message_delta as the response streams, changing nothing, and reports them when the stream ends or is cut off. Usage is known only after the response, so a user can overrun by one call and go into debt.The sentinel is a service layer: an out-of-process addon that each model call streams through over a WebSocket. It turns every tool call in a model response into an inspect_sentinel BeforeToolCall step and runs the configured sentinel on it. It sits below the quota layer, so what the quota layer meters is what the client got. Whatever any layer passes on, the rules judge again, and they allow exactly one request, POST /v1/messages on the model host. The rule's condition is the one the quota and the sentinel run on (a YAML anchor in roxy.yaml), so a request those layers skip, /v1/messages/ say, is one the rules deny rather than a model call that went unmetered and unjudged.
35.title: What just happened

36.text: roxy enrols once with a token, keeps the node token it is issued in its state dir, and polls the control plane for its lease: the whole roxy.yaml, the values of the secrets it declares as lease: true, and how to ship the flow log (node mode). controlplane/controlplane.py is the server side of the node protocol in one file. It turns model_key: { env: MODEL_API_KEY } into a lease secret from its own environment, and its lease_id is a hash of the config and secrets, so editing roxy.yaml changes the lease and roxy applies it on its next poll. Its enrolment token stays valid across restarts, because roxy's state dir is tmpfs and every docker compose up re-enrols; a real control plane consumes a token on first use. To run roxy from the file instead, with no control plane: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.standalone.yaml up --build --attach traffic
36.title: Node mode

37.text: A layer that cannot do its job (the auth service unreachable, the quota board answering something that is not an allowance, the sentinel unable to read a response) fails the exchange: roxy answers 503 naming the layer and logs a layer_error. The quota layer reads a non-streamed response whole to find its usage, and one over 8 MiB fails the same way; aborted streams are charged for the usage seen before the abort. Stop the quota board (docker compose stop quota-board) to see it.
37.title: Failure is closed

38.text: The sentinel runs deny_regex from policies.py, which searches <tool name> <arguments as JSON> for a regular expression. The default catches curl, wget, nc, ncat, ssh, scp, rsync and rm -rf. Set your own with SENTINEL_DENY: SENTINEL_DENY='\bls\b' docker compose up --attach traffic Any inspect_sentinel monitor or protocol works in its place: set SENTINEL to its module:attribute, and for one that asks a model, SENTINEL_MONITOR_MODEL and a route out (add the sentinel service to the egress network). The sidecar is in sentinel/.
38.title: The denylist

39.text:
Any HTTP client that honours HTTP_PROXY can take the clients' place; the proxy is on 127.0.0.1:3128. Claude Code, against the scripted model: HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:3128 \
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://fake-model:8080 \
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=placeholder \
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS='x-roxy-auth: alice-secret' \
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 \
claude To point the stack at the real API, allow api.anthropic.com in the rules, set the real key as the model_key secret, and trust roxy's CA (http://127.0.0.1:3130/roxy-ca.pem) in the client, since roxy then terminates TLS. The client follows HTTP_PROXY because it chooses to; any process can ignore it. To contain an agent, run it where its only route out is roxy (sandbox containment).
39.title: Using it with a real client

41.text:
Addons are listed under addons:, in the order they wrap the exchange
(addon model). Each entry is a WASM layer or a
service layer; the two kinds share most keys. addons:

    kind: wasm
    path: /etc/roxy/addons/sentinel.wasm
    mode: enforce
    when: host == "api.anthropic.com" and path starts_with "/v1/messages"
    subscribe: { request: full, response: head }
    capabilities: [state, record, endpoints]

        url: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
        headers: { x-api-key: "${secret:monitor_key}" }
        timeout: 10s
      threat-intel:
        url: https://ti.internal:8443/score
        path: prefix
        private_ok: true
    limits: { max_memory: 128mb, first_byte_timeout: 30s }
    config: { reject_at: 0.8 }

  - name: monitor
    kind: service
    endpoint: sidecar
    mode: observe
    sample: 0.1
    subscribe: { request: head, response: head }
    endpoints:
      sidecar: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:9000/layer", private_ok: true }
    limits: { first_byte_timeout: 2s, max_connections: 4, max_streams: 100 }

43.title: endpoints

44.text:
Limits catch a broken layer, not a slow one: a slow layer makes its
exchanges slow, not denied, with one exception. Exchanges that keep every
instance busy past first_byte_timeout cost the exchanges queued behind
them, which are denied rather than wait (max_instances below). Each is
optional. keykinddefaultwhat it boundsfirst_byte_timeoutboth30show long a layer may hold a head, request or response, before passing it on or answering: its own time only (starting an instance, its work, endpoint calls, reading the body it was given), never time next spends waiting for upstream. Overrun fails the layer closed (budget:first_byte_timeout for a WASM layer, service:timeout for a service layer), and the exchange with it in enforce mode. A service layer gets one budget to obtain a stream and a fresh one when the upstream outcome reaches it, including a headless end, until it has answered; an observing one gets a last from roxy's final message to its own end of the stream. It bounds the layer's own time, not the exchange's: body-idle and upstream timeouts still apply while the answer clock is suspended (service layers). It also bounds the wait for an instance when all max_instances are busy, on its own: an enforce exchange that gets none within it is denied (layer_error, no_instance); an observer loses its copy (observer_lagged, no_instance)max_memorywasm64mblinear memory per instance, summed over the instance's memories; table growth and the host resource table (4096 live resources: body streams, pollables, pending responses) are capped too. What a layer holds of a body lives here. An interpreter in WASM (Python) needs 128–256 MiBmax_instanceswasm1024live instances, so concurrent exchanges and, with max_memory, the layer's memory. An exchange that finds none free waits first_byte_timeout for one, then fails closed (no_instance), so the clients holding every instance cannot queue the rest indefinitely. Instances start on demandrecycle_after_exchangeswasm10000an instance is replaced after this many exchanges; 0 replaces it after every exchangerecycle_above_memorywasmthree quarters of max_memoryan instance whose memory passed this is replaced after its exchange. Bodies may stream for
longer, subject to the client's and upstream's body idle timeouts. The
client edge applies response_body_idle_timeout even when consuming an
internal body that HEAD or a bodiless status prevents it from sending.
WebSockets have the relay's idle timeout. There is no total CPU budget:
a guest yields on an engine-wide 1 ms tick so other tasks can run and
cancellation can stop it.

47.text:
A layer has no access outside its own streams. capabilities grants it
named host services, which a WASM layer calls
and a service layer sends as messages: capabilitygrantsendpointsendpoints.call: outbound calls to the layer's named endpoints, with roxy attaching the headersstateflow.state-get, flow.state-put: the state store the rules userecordflow.record: structured events in the flow logmetricsflow.metric-get: read a metric for this flow's keylogflow.log: roxy's operational logquarantineflow.quarantine: put the whole proxy into quarantine; enforce only Every import is linked whatever is granted (one binary runs under any

47.title: Capabilities

48.text:
subscribe names what the layer gets of each direction. With full (the
default) the layer owns that direction: it reads the body, chunk by chunk,
and what it passes on is the body that goes on. With head the layer gets
the head with an empty body and no content-length, and the body bypasses
it: whatever the layer passes on (the head it gives next, or the head it
answers with) carries the body it did not see, spliced on by roxy. An enforce layer can still deny, rewrite or answer at a head it is
subscribed to; the bodies stream past it at no cost in copies or
buffering.A response head-only layer answers with the status it was given to pass
the response on with its head edited; the body from upstream follows. Any
other status is an answer of the layer's own: its body stands and the
body from upstream is dropped, so a layer can refuse at the response head.
A layer that answers without next resolving answers whole too, since
there is no body from upstream.A layer that passes on bytes of a body it is not subscribed to fails the
exchange closed: a 503 before the response head, a cut body after it,
layer_error with kind: unsubscribed:request or
unsubscribed:response. An open lane has unknown length on the wire,
including a bypassed body. HTTP/1.1 uses chunked framing so a later cut
remains visible after the last declared byte; any declared length still
validates the body.A head-only observer gets copies of the heads and no copy of the body,
so neither the lag budget nor the buffer budget is touched for it.The rules are not affected: they judge the request that leaves the
stack, head and body, whoever supplied each.Bodies are decoded for the layers, and a WebSocket relayed without
extensions, only when some layer that runs is subscribed to a body
(content codings, WebSockets).
48.title: What a layer sees

49.text:
Lanes carry HTTP structure: one head, streaming body bytes, optional
trailers, then an end or cut. They resemble an HTTP/2 stream's lifecycle;
they are not HTTP/2 wire streams. Request and response lanes are independent,
so a layer can answer while it holds a request, or keep answering while it
holds an upstream response for approval. protocol or featuresupport and limitsSSE, NDJSON, streaming JSON, multipart responses and HTTP-based MCPbodies stream as bytes. Chunk boundaries need not match application messages; a layer editing them must parse the application's framinggRPCthe lanes support concurrent request and response bodies and trailers such as grpc-status. Service layers can receive and send trailers explicitly. The Python helper exposes received trailers but its forwarding methods do not send them. WASM host-side body.passthrough preserves trailers, but the WASI byte streams do not expose trailers for reading or rewriting; copying bytes into a new stream does not preserve them. Head-only subscriptions keep the bypassed body's trailersWebSocketsHTTP/1.1 upgrades are supported; bodies then carry raw WebSocket frames. WebSocket over HTTP/2 extended CONNECT is not enabledinformational heads, including 103 Early Hintsupstream informational responses are not relayed, with or without addons. Addons cannot publish informational heads before their final head (HTTP)arbitrary upgrades and TCP tunnelsonly WebSocket upgrades are adapted into addon lanes. CONNECT on the proxy listener establishes an inspected HTTP/TLS connection, not an arbitrary addon-controlled tunnelWebTransport, CONNECT-UDP and MASQUEnot supported: datagrams and sessions containing multiple streams need semantics beyond these ordered byte lanes. HTTP/3 is not a supported transport For SSE approval, a full-body layer can publish a 200 text/event-stream
head and send a start event or comment such as : approval pending\n\n.
It can keep sending comments while it holds the request or buffers selected
upstream events. Once approved, it forwards the request or writes the
approved or edited events into its existing response body, then streams
subsequent events. A refusal after that head is an application event in
the same response, not a new HTTP status. A second response head fails the
layer and cuts an answer already in progress. Keepalive bytes must reach the client within its idle timeout and roxy's
response_body_idle_timeout. They do not extend a client's absolute
deadline, an endpoint-call timeout, or an upstream timeout. SSE comments
are valid only for an SSE body; gRPC requires correctly framed gRPC
messages, and its HTTP/2 PING is connection control rather than body data.
49.title: Streaming protocols

50.text:
when is a rule language condition over admission
fields. A layer runs only on the exchanges it matches; the rest pass it at
no cost (no instance, no body pumping, no service session). when sees the request as it reaches the layer: what the downstream layer
passed on, re-validated. A downstream layer can steer a request into or
out of an upstream layer's when.It may read admission fields, headers, the query, state[..], metric.<id>
and address lists. body.*, response.* and ws.* are config errors.tag["x"] sees tags set by enforce layers downstream, not the rules' tags
(the rules run upstream of the layers).An unavailable input (a metric, an address list, a missing value under an
operator that cannot answer for null) fails the flow closed like a
layer failure (503, layer_error with kind: when:<code>), never
skips the layer. On an observe layer the failure is logged and the layer
gets no copy.A layer when skipped on a WebSocket's upgrade request is not in that
WebSocket's byte path. sample (observe only) is drawn from the flow id, so it is the same for a
flow however often it is asked.
50.title: Choosing exchanges

51.text:
The stack is a chain of stages joined by lanes
(addon model):
the client edge adapts the HTTP/1.1 connection or HTTP/2 stream and puts the
client's request on the first lane, each layer runs on its own task, and
the core stage validates the forwarded request, evaluates admission and
in-flight rules, applies destination restrictions, and owns the upstream
connection and any WebSocket relay. A layer's answer goes to the client
as soon as the layer gives it; a forwarded request continues upstream
while the layer waits for its response. The flow is logged once every lane is terminal,
its body has been read or discarded, and all drivers, input pumps, upload
monitors and enforcing host-service workers have finished, including
destruction after cancellation. The transport observes client loss through
reclamation. Upstream upload accounting completes before the core releases
the context. Sending an early response does not bypass this barrier. HTTP/1.1 does not accept
the next request until this work finishes, even if a layer has ended both
of its lanes but its handler or host-service calls are still running. Once a layer is done with the client's upload, the rest of it is dropped:
on HTTP/1.1 the codec drains or closes as it does after a deny
(HTTP), on HTTP/2 the stream is reset
with no error. What a layer passes on is re-validated as strictly as a client request:
an absolute http(s) URI; host, hop-by-hop and framing fields refused
at the boundary (roxy derives them); the workload's limits applied. A
WASM layer may not set content-length either (the body carries its own
length); a service layer may, and the body it sends is held to it
(service layers). chain.next
fills in the scheme and authority from the exchange when the layer
leaves them unset.The response reaching the client edge must be final; a 1xx other than
the 101 of a relayed upgrade fails closed as invalid_response.What next returns is a response whoever produced it: the upstream's,
the rules' refusal, or a 503 layer:<name> generated for a failure
upstream, recorded on the flow as that refusal. The layer may pass it on
or reshape it. A cut forward or an upstream lane ending without a head
returns an error from next without making the layer faulty. A failed
client request instead cancels the exchange.A layer's response body to the client waits for the flow log like every
forwarded body (audit backpressure).Layers compile at config load and are cached across reloads while their
file and settings are unchanged, so instance pools stay warm. A reload
swaps the stack for new exchanges; exchanges in flight finish on theirs. In the flow log: fieldwith addonsaddonsthe layers that ran, in stack order; a layer its when or sample skipped is not in itrules, decision, terminal_rulethe rules' decision on the request that left the stack; req is what the client sent. Metric keys (for the rules' samples and metric-get) also come from the request that left. A layer whose next returned the rules' 403 and then answered 200 itself is logged decision: deny, res.status: 200decision: answered, terminal_rule: layer:<name>a layer answered itself, whatever its status: the layer nearest the client whose response lane upstream had no head when its own answer's head landed, decided then. A forward it kept reading the response of runs to its end, and the record keeps what the rules decided of it; one it stopped reading the response of is cancelled upstream, with reason: upstream_aborted; a forward it cut itself gets reason: forward_aborted. If a layer fails before publishing its answer, the generated refusal is the decision, deny, whatever a downstream layer makes of it. If it fails after its answer reaches the client, the answer remains recorded and its body is cut503, terminal_rule: layer:<name>, reason: layer_errora layer failed before the response head; the connection is closed and a layer_error event follows with kind one of trap, budget:<limit>, capability:<name>, invalid_request, invalid_response, no_response, unsubscribed:<direction>, ... After the head, the body is cut (HTTP/1.1 breaks the connection, HTTP/2 resets the stream) and layer_error follows. Which layer, if any, is one rule (who is blamed) If a layer fails while handling a denial the core already made, its generated
503 still travels downstream, but the flow record keeps the original deny's
terminal_rule and reason. A downstream layer reshaping that response does
not change the recorded denial. The layer failure has its own layer_error
event.
51.title: In the proxy

52.text:
On a flow some layer runs on and is subscribed to the body, roxy decodes
the client's request body as the first such layer gets it and the response
before it reaches the first subscribed layer on its way downstream, removing content-encoding;
the body's length becomes unknown. A body no running layer is subscribed
to is not decoded, and reaches the upstream or the client as sent. The client gets an uncompressed response and the upstream an
uncompressed request body; the origin's response to roxy stays
compressed. Nothing re-encodes.The codings and their strictness are the rules'
(HTTP). Data that does not decode, or
a decoded body over limits.max_request_body_bytes or
limits.max_response_body_bytes, cuts the exchange like any failed body,
also on a flow only an observer runs on.A body in a coding roxy does not know passes through as it is, with its
content-encoding; so does a 206 or any response with content-range.The rules upstream of the layers read the response first and decode it
for themselves (body rules).No extension (permessage-deflate above all) is negotiated on a
WebSocket a body-subscribed layer runs on (WebSockets). http.decode_for_addons: false turns this off: layers see the bytes as
sent, with their content-encoding, and WebSockets negotiate whatever
extensions client and upstream agree on.
52.title: Content codings

53.text:
A layer gets the upgrade request in handle and passes it on with next
(a service layer forwards it on its stream); the response from upstream is the
101. After it, the request body carries the client's bytes and the
response body the upstream's for as long as the WebSocket is open. A layer
reads, rewrites or holds back either direction as any body, refuses the
upgrade by answering without next, and is left out of the WebSocket when
its when skips the upgrade request. A subscription to one body puts the
layer in that direction only: the other's bytes flow past it, however long
its handler lives on relaying the direction it is in. A layer that turns the upstream's 101 into another status fails the
exchange closed (503 from layer:<name>) and roxy closes the upstream
WebSocket; a 101 with no upgrade from upstream fails closed too.Only Upgrade: websocket is an upgrade for the layers. A request asking
for any other upgrade (h2c, say) is an ordinary request roxy forwards
once it strips the upgrade, with its body and the usual body cap.The bodies carry raw WebSocket frames. Frames from the client are masked,
so their payload reads as sent only from the upstream's side.A layer must stream both bodies at once: the request body ends only when
the client closes, while the response streams all along (the
roxy-addon SDK does this). Holding bytes back until more arrive stalls
an interactive protocol.The layer's head deadline does not limit the relayed bodies; the relay's
idle timeout still applies. When the relay ends, roxy closes the
client's connection whether or not the layers have ended their bodies;
bytes already on their way get a second to arrive.
53.title: WebSockets

54.text:
Every failure is closed. A trap, an exceeded budget, a second next
or respond, a missing capability, a host failure, a head the host
refuses, a body stream that is not the host's, a missing response, bytes
on an unsubscribed body, a handler that returns still holding a body
stream or a pending response, or a cancelled exchange is a
LayerError: a 503 on the lane downstream of the layer before the
response head (recorded as a deny, whatever a layer there makes of it),
a cut body after it.A client that gives up cancels the exchange. The guest is stopped,
its instance discarded, the slot freed. No layer_error is logged.No clean end for a failed body. A guest body ends with an error once
its exchange has failed; a response body the guest produces (bytes or a
stream) holds its end until the handler returns, so a trap after the last
byte still cuts it. An open lane has unknown wire length, even for an
empty declared body, until its producer ends cleanly. HEAD and bodiless
statuses commit at the head, but their internal bodies must still finish
within the body idle timeout. A streamed body is complete only through
finish: dropped unfinished, it is cut where it
stopped, the layer's own doing (reason: forward_aborted or
answer_aborted), not a failure.A cut forward gets no response. A request body passed to next that
the guest drops without finish is cut at the upstream, and nothing
comes back for it: next fails for the guest (error.internal), which
may answer itself, and its answer stands. A body the guest passed through
that fails behind it (the client gave up) is cut the same way, at the
client's fault.An instance that failed its exchange is discarded, never reused.Layers see canonical heads and body streams, never wire bytes, and have
no filesystem, sockets or environment: all their I/O is next,
endpoints and flow.

57.text:

session) within a client connection. Each has a ULID.Canonical: roxy's validated, normalised, version-agnostic HTTP model.Admission rule / in-flight rule: decided before the request is

58.text:
One YAML file, version: 1. Each section is described on the page the

listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy      # the default; `http` serves origin-form requests directly
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128

secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline stripped
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control-plane lease; standalone `run` refuses it

metrics:
  - id: github_writes
    count: requests
    where: host under "api.github.com" and method in [POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE]
    key: [client.ip]
    window: 1m

rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: openai

    then:

60.text:
Checked in order per candidate IP; the first hit is the reason: deny_cidrs: never valid, nothing opts out.With deny_private_ranges (default true): the ranges below, except
addresses in allow_cidrs and flows whose allow rule says
private_ok: true.Every list in deny_lists: never valid, nothing opts out. class (private_range:<class>)rangesunspecified0.0.0.0/8, ::private10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 (RFC 1918)shared100.64/10 (CGNAT)loopback127/8, ::1link_local169.254/16, fe80::/10documentation192.0.2/24, 198.51.100/24, 203.0.113/24, 2001:db8::/32benchmarking198.18/15multicast224/4, ff00::/8reserved192.0.0/24, 240/4unique_localfc00::/7site_localfec0::/10discard100::/64 Denies match every form of an address: as given, IPv4-mapped,

61.text:

and as @name in rules. address_lists:

    file: /etc/roxy/lists/blocked.txt    # one IPv4/IPv6 CIDR or address per line; `#` comments

    inline: [169.254.169.254/32, "fd00:ec2::254/128", 100.100.100.200/32] Representation. Two sorted tables of disjoint CIDR blocks per list,
one per family, binary-searched: 8 bytes per IPv4 block, 32 per IPv6, no
allocation per lookup (a million IPv4 plus 100k IPv6 entries: about
11 MiB, tens of nanoseconds). Nested and duplicate entries merge. A
malformed line is an error naming file and line; a malformed inline entry
is reported at address_lists[i].inline[j]. A file over
limits.max_address_list_bytes (256 MiB), or not valid UTF-8, is a load
error.Matching. The deny floor matches every form
(above), since matching more
is the safe direction for a deny. Rule membership (ip
in @list) is exact, with only the IPv4-mapped equivalence, since a rule
may allow on it: client.ip in @internal must not treat a 6to4 address
embedding an internal IPv4 address as internal.In rules. @name works wherever a CIDR does: right of in / not
in with an ip field. An undefined list is a compile error.Reload. List files are watched with the config. A changed file is
recompiled and swapped with the policy, and upstream pools are flushed,
so a pooled connection to a newly denied IP is never reused. An exchange
in flight keeps its policy, pools and lists, and can still open a
connection the new lists would deny; the next exchange on the connection
uses the new lists.roxy check reports each list's entry count. roxy rule test loads
lists as roxy run would; if one fails to load it warns and treats every
@list as unavailable, so a rule reading one fails closed.

68.title: Events

69.text:
Every injected secret value is scrubbed from any logged string, the
operational log (tracing) included: a string is redacted once, with the
secret generation the exchange loaded, and that one copy goes to every
sink. Values of authorization, proxy-authorization, cookie,
set-cookie and x-api-key are never logged; log.redact_headers adds
more. Query values are redacted.
69.title: Redaction

70.text:
The write path never drops a record while roxy runs
(audit backpressure). One writer per destination. Emitters serialise each event on their
own thread and enqueue the bytes; one writer thread owns the file and
writes everything queued in one batch. The writer waits a moment for
more records before each write, so a burst is one write and a record is
written within a couple of milliseconds of being emitted.Backpressure. Emitting never blocks or drops. Once unwritten bytes
pass log.flow.high_water (8 MiB) the log reports not ready and every
traffic producer waits for it: each new client connection, exchange and
HTTP/2 stream, each forwarded body chunk and each WebSocket read. A
failing destination (disk full, I/O error) holds traffic the same way, and
is reported.Rotation happens at a batch boundary, so a record never spans two
files: the file is renamed to <path>.<UTC timestamp>-<seq>, a new one
is opened, files beyond max_files are deleted (oldest first), and
rotated files are optionally gzipped in the background. Names sort in
rotation order even across a restart on a clock behind the previous run's:
a rotation on a clock behind the newest existing name reuses its stamp
with a higher sequence. Only files of that name shape count towards
max_files or are deleted. A
failed rotation is a failed write: traffic is held and it is retried.
SIGHUP reopens the file, for external rotation.Shutdown. Everything queued is written before exit, with up to 10
seconds of retries for a failing destination; whatever is still unwritten
when roxy then exits is lost, and an error logged. This is the one point
at which a record can be dropped.Durability. Each batch is flushed to the operating system, and
max_file_bytes checked, at the batch boundary. roxy does not fsync: a
roxy crash loses nothing queued; a kernel crash or power loss can lose
batches the OS had not yet written to disk. log:
  redact_headers: []
  flow:
    path: /var/log/roxy/flow.jsonl  # absent = stdout
    connection_events: false
    ws_message_every: 0             # also log every Nth WebSocket message; 0 = denied only
    high_water: 8mb                 # at least 64kb
    max_file_bytes: 100mb           # absent = never rotate; at least 4kb
    max_files: 10                   # absent = keep all; at least 1
    compress: true roxy check refuses max_file_bytes, max_files or compress without
path (stdout cannot rotate), and max_files or compress without
max_file_bytes. The same floors apply under log.capture. roxy's own operational logs go to stderr through tracing: --log-format
json|pretty and --log-level (or RUST_LOG).
70.title: Writing

71.text:
roxy tees the heads and bodies of exchanges, exactly as forwarded, to
<capture_dir>/capture.rxc: those an admission rule selects with capture:
request | response | both, or every forwarded exchange with
log.capture.all: true. Capture is decided at admission and covers
the exchange from its first byte; the taps sit after the in-flight rules
allowed a chunk. WebSocket relays are captured both ways at the relay next
to the upstream, not as an addon layer changes them for the client. Capture is written like the flow log (one writer, batching, rotation,
backpressure). Injected secret values are scrubbed from every string of a
captured head (URL, header names and values); nothing else is: the
header-name redaction above is flow-log only, and bodies are captured
unredacted. capture_dir: /var/lib/roxy/capture   # absent = capture disabled; restart to change
log:
  capture:
    all: false
    high_water: 64mb
    max_file_bytes: 1gb
    max_files: 20
    compress: true
limits:
  max_capture_body_bytes: 16mb       # per direction per exchange Every log.capture setting needs capture_dir; roxy check reports
settings given without it.
71.title: Capture

72.title: Capture format

73.text:
Everything a layer can do outside its own streams, each a capability
granted in config
(capabilities). A WASM
layer calls them as the flow and endpoints imports named here; a
service layer sends the matching messages on its stream
(service layers), except
endpoints.call, which a service does for itself. Both reach one host, so
a call means the same and fails the same way for either kind. The caps on
each (payload sizes, calls in flight, key length) are in
fixed caps.
73.title: Host services

74.text:
endpoints.call(name, head, body): roxy resolves the name to the configured
URL, attaches the endpoint's headers (replacing any the layer set), applies
the timeout, and enforces the address floor and deny lists. The
layer cannot name a destination and never sees the credentials. Calls do not
pass through the layer stack, so a monitor's own model call cannot recurse
through it; the response goes back to the layer, not through the rules. Each call emits an endpoint_call flow event. An exchange has at most 8 calls in flight. A further endpoints.call
waits for one of them to be answered before it returns, and before roxy
takes the call's body: a waiting call holds nothing.The request body is buffered before the call (at most 16 MiB), and
reading it counts against the timeout.An unknown name, a denied address, a refused path, a timeout and a
failure reach the layer as distinct error variants
(destination-not-found, destination-denied, request-uri-invalid,
timeout, internal), through the pending-response the call returns. The endpoint's path setting: pathtargetfixed (default)the configured URL is the whole target; the request's path and query are ignoredprefixthe request's path, normalised (percent-encodings canonicalised, . segments removed), is appended under the configured path; its query follows the endpoint's own. A percent-encoded slash or backslash (%2F, %5C) is refused A segment that starts with .., in any percent-encoded spelling and
whatever follows the dots (..;x, which an origin that strips path
parameters reads as ..), is refused in both modes: the call fails with
request-uri-invalid, nothing is dialled, and the endpoint_call
event records the refusal. Under prefix, text a layer
reflects into the path can pick any route below the configured path, with
roxy's credential attached.
74.title: Endpoints (endpoints)

75.text:
flow.state-get / flow.state-put: the state store
the rules read as state["key"] and write with set_state. A key a layer
writes is the key a rule reads, so a layer can leave a mark for a rule to
deny on, and read what a rule left. Values are strings; a layer that wants
state["k"] == "yes" to match writes yes. A state-put without a TTL
gets the store's default (one hour). A miss returns none. A key over
1 KiB or a value over 64 KiB returns an error to the layer. A write when
the store is full fails the exchange closed, as it does a rule's
set_state; nothing is evicted. Only an enforce layer may write: a
state-put from an observer fails the layer (layer_error, kind host)
and the exchange goes on, like add-tag, since the store steers every
flow's rules. The store survives a reload, under
limits.max_state_entries.
75.title: State (state)

76.text:
flow.current(): the flow id, connection id, tags, and the principal as
roxy established it (client IP, listener, TLS SNI). Key per-principal state
on these, not on client-supplied session headers. flow.config() is the
layer's config: value as a JSON document. A service gets both in its
open message.
76.title: Identity and config

77.text:
flow.record(kind, json) writes a layer_record event to the flow
log with the flow id, layer name and timestamp. kind and every string
value in the document pass through the secret redactor; a document that
is not JSON fails the exchange. The call
waits while the flow log is behind and is never dropped.
77.title: Record (record)

78.text:
flow.metric-get(id, []) reads a metric for this flow's own key (the key
fields evaluated on the request that left the addon stack); explicit key
values are refused. A key with no entry reads none (a rule reads the same
key as 0); an unknown id, or a key field the request does not have, fails
the exchange. flow.log writes to roxy's operational log with the
flow id and layer name.
78.title: Metrics and log (metrics, log)

79.text:
flow.quarantine() puts the whole proxy into
quarantine: the exchange it was called on
is refused _quarantined (nothing of it is forwarded, whatever the layer
answers), and so is every exchange after it, until an operator or the
control plane lifts it. It is for what a layer is sure must stop the
workload; one bad request is denied by answering it. Only an enforce layer
may call it: from an observer it fails the layer (layer_error, kind
host) and the exchange goes on, like add-tag. The
quarantined flow event's cause is kind: layer with the layer's name and
the flow. A config whose layers hold the capability needs roxy run
--state-dir, as one with a quarantine rule does. A layer cannot
terminate a client: it denies the exchange.
79.title: Quarantine (quarantine)

80.text:
How clients talk to roxy, how requests are parsed and canonicalised, and
what goes to the upstream and back.
80.title: HTTP

81.text:
modethe client speaksrequest targethttp_proxy (default)HTTP/1.1 to a proxy (HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY)absolute-form, or CONNECT and then origin-form inside the tunnelhttpplain HTTP/1.1 to roxy as if it were the serverorigin-form; Host names the target Each mode accepts one protocol and closes anything else. roxy does not
authenticate clients; rules see listener.name and client.ip. listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy           # the default
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
    quarantine_on:             # optional; off when absent
      parse_errors: { count: 20, window: 1m }
  - name: gateway
    mode: http
    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
    forwarded_for:             # optional; without it X-Forwarded-For is ignored
      trusted_hops: 1          # the proxies in front of roxy: here, one load balancer quarantine_on.parse_errors puts the whole process into
quarantine once the listener has logged
count parse errors within window (count at least 1, window a whole
number of seconds, at least 1s). It counts a client sending what roxy will not parse, not one that
is slow or leaves. Setting it needs roxy run --state-dir. forwarded_for.trusted_hops (at least 1; mode: http only) names the
client from X-Forwarded-For (below).
81.title: Listener modes

82.text:
Absolute-form (GET http://host/path HTTP/1.1): plain HTTP; Host
must equal the URI authority.CONNECT: a tunnel roxy inspects (below).Origin-form: rejected, except to roxy.internal, which serves the CA
certificate at /roxy-ca.pem
(CA distribution) and 404
for anything else.Proxy-Authorization is hop-by-hop: dropped, never forwarded.
82.title: HTTP proxy

83.text:
For a gateway behind a TLS-terminating load balancer
(HTTP gateway). Only origin-form. Absolute-form, CONNECT and * are refused
(target_form_mismatch; bad_request_target for *) and the connection
closed.The target is Host: required, exactly one (missing_host,
multiple_host, bad_authority), port 80 unless given, scheme http.
Hosts may differ between requests on one connection.Without a redirect the upstream is the Host authority over plain
HTTP; redirect with scheme: https sends it on over TLS.roxy.internal is a host like any other.A TLS handshake is closed at the record header (tls_on_http_listener).
83.title: HTTP listener

84.text:
Without forwarded_for, client.ip is the TCP peer: behind a load
balancer, the load balancer. With forwarded_for.trusted_hops: N, each of
the N proxies in front of roxy is taken to append the address it accepted
the connection from to X-Forwarded-For, so the client is the Nth entry
from the right of the header (every X-Forwarded-For line joined in
order). Entries to its left are the client's own and are never read. That address is client.ip in rules, metric keys and the flow log, and
the addon principal's client_ip: roxy has one notion of the client.
The flow log keeps the TCP peer as client.peer for forensics
(flow log).Each request is resolved on its own: a kept-alive connection from a load
balancer carries many clients.A request with fewer entries than hops, a trusted entry that is not a
bare IPv4 or IPv6 address (a port, brackets, a zone, unknown, an
obfuscated identifier), or a header over 4 KiB in all is refused as a
request roxy cannot parse: 400, reason forwarded_for_invalid, the
connection closed, counted by quarantine_on.parse_errors. It is never
attributed to the peer: a bypassed or misconfigured load balancer must
neither let a client choose its address nor fold every client into one.An IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (::ffff:a.b.c.d), as an entry or as the
peer of a dual-stack [::] listener, is the IPv4 address it embeds, as a
host literal is.The header goes upstream as received; roxy neither appends the peer nor
strips it.limits.max_connections_per_client is applied when the connection is
accepted, before any header, so it counts the peer
(limits). A hop count says how the header was built; it does not prove a connection
came through those proxies. A client that can reach the listener directly
can write N well-formed entries and choose its client.ip, so the
listener must be reachable only from the trusted proxies, which is the
network's claim to make (a security group, a private subnet), as
containment is (threat model). The setting is refused on an http_proxy listener: the requests inside a
CONNECT tunnel carry whatever X-Forwarded-For the client wrote, and no
proxy in front of roxy can add to them.
84.title: Clients behind a load balancer

85.text:
A CONNECT gets 200 Connection Established; decisions are made on the
requests inside the tunnel. The tunnel's first bytes must be: A TLS ClientHello
(ClientHello sniffing). With
tls.require_sni_match (default true) the SNI must name the CONNECT host,
compared canonicalised (sni_mismatch); an unusable SNI is closed
(bad_sni); no SNI means the CONNECT host. roxy terminates TLS with a
leaf for that host; the inner protocol is HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 by ALPN.Plaintext HTTP, only with http.allow_plain_in_connect (default
false). Anything else is closed; raw TCP never passes. Inside a tunnel, requests
are origin-form and their Host (or :authority) must match the CONNECT
host, port-normalised, whatever the SNI said.
85.title: CONNECT

86.text:
Inside a TLS tunnel, by ALPN (http.enable_h2, default true). The h2
crate parses it; the same semantic validation as HTTP/1.1 follows
(HTTP/2 requests). Upstream, roxy offers
h2 and http/1.1 and serialises as whichever the origin negotiates: the
canonical authority goes out as host over HTTP/1.1 and as :authority
alone over HTTP/2, never both. WebSocket upgrades always use HTTP/1.1
(WebSockets).
86.title: HTTP/2

87.text:
Upstream informational responses such as 103 Early Hints are not relayed
to the client, whether or not addons are enabled. The upstream HTTP client
consumes them and returns the final response. Roxy generates its own
100 Continue when admitting an upload; it does not forward the origin's
100. A WebSocket 101 Switching Protocols is handled separately as an
upgrade. Addon response lanes carry one final head. They cannot publish 103 and
then a final response. An addon that starts a synthetic 200 streaming
response has committed that status and those headers; it may subsequently
use upstream body bytes, but cannot replace the head.
87.title: Informational responses

88.text:
Two settings, one per direction. http.allow_response_trailers (default
true) forwards an origin's response trailers to the client, as HTTP/2
trailers or as the trailer section of a chunked HTTP/1.1 response (a
response with a declared length cannot carry them). gRPC, which puts the
call's outcome in grpc-status, works by default.
http.allow_request_trailers (default false) accepts trailers on requests,
HTTP/2 trailers or a chunked trailer section; without it a request that
carries them is refused with reason trailers. Request trailers arrive
after the rules have decided, so they stay opt-in. In either direction a
trailer section may not carry framing, routing, authentication or
content-* fields (authorization, cookie, set-cookie, range,
max-forwards, cache-control, every hop-by-hop name): on a request that
is a rejection, on a response the body is cut before the client sees it
complete. A body a rule or addon buffers to read keeps its trailers. Request trailers reach an origin only over h2: HTTP/1.1 needs the names
in a Trailer header before the body. Trailers to an HTTP/1.1 origin fail
with reason trailers (400 and close on HTTP/1.1, a stream reset on
HTTP/2) before the origin sees the request complete, for as long as any
HTTP/1.1 connection to that origin is open or pooled (hyper keeps idle
connections about 90 s), including one opened for a request held to
HTTP/1.1.
88.title: Trailers

89.text:
The client-facing HTTP/1.1 codec is roxy's own (on httparse for
tokenising): ambiguities RFC 9112 lets a server resolve are rejected. pub struct CanonicalRequest {
    pub method: Method,        // validated token
    pub scheme: Scheme,        // Http | Https
    pub authority: Authority,  // host (DNS name | IPv4 | IPv6), port always explicit
    pub path: Path,            // normalised, see below
    pub query: Option<Query>,  // validated raw bytes, parsed pairs for matching
    pub headers: Headers,      // lowercase names, ordered, validated, hop-by-hop removed
    pub body: Body,            // a stream; its known length, if any, decides upstream framing
    pub meta: RequestMeta,     // client version, receipt time, head size, target form, expect/upgrade
}
89.title: Canonical request

90.text:
A violation closes the connection, not just the request, and emits a
parse_error flow event with a stable reason code. The knobs live under
http: and default to strict. The header and body rules are one implementation, applied to every request
roxy judges: an HTTP/1.1 head, an HTTP/2 stream, and what a service layer
passes on. Each path adds only its own wire rules ahead of them (line
structure for HTTP/1.1, pseudo-headers and connection-specific fields for
HTTP/2, the fields a layer may not set), so a field list one path refuses
the others refuse for the same reason.
90.title: Rejection rules

91.text:
The method is a token of at most 32 bytes.The target form fits the context: absolute-form on the proxy port,
origin-form in a tunnel or on an http listener, authority-form only for
CONNECT on the proxy port.The version is exactly HTTP/1.1. HTTP/1.0 needs http.allow_http10
and its connection closes after the response whatever Connection says;
HTTP/0.9 is never accepted. A response of unknown length to an HTTP/1.0
client is close-delimited: the body ends when roxy closes the connection.
If the upstream body is cut short (upstream error, size cap, timeout,
forbidden trailer) roxy closes the connection all the same, so the client
cannot tell a cut body from a complete one. roxy still logs the failure.Lines end in CRLF; a bare LF or CR anywhere in the head is rejected.Head at most limits.max_header_bytes (64 KiB); URL at most
limits.max_url_bytes (8 KiB).
91.title: Request line

92.text:
Names are tokens, no whitespace before the colon, no obs-fold.Values are visible ASCII, SP and HTAB, surrounding whitespace stripped.
CR, LF, NUL and other controls are rejected; non-ASCII needs
http.allow_obs_text, under which the rules read each such byte as the
ISO-8859-1 character of the same value
(comparison).At most limits.max_headers (100) fields.Exactly one Host, matching the URI authority (absolute-form) or the
CONNECT host (tunnel); on an http listener it names the target. An
HTTP/1.0 absolute-form request may omit it.A host is a DNS name of A-labels, a strict dotted-quad IPv4 literal or a
bracketed IPv6 literal. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal ([::ffff:a.b.c.d])
is the IPv4 address it embeds and is parsed, matched, logged and
forwarded as a.b.c.d.At most one Content-Length, digits only, at most 19 digits; a duplicate
is rejected even with equal values. A non-zero length declared for a body
that has already ended (a layer passing content-length with an empty
body) is bad_content_length, not an empty body.Transfer-Encoding, if present, is exactly chunked: one field, one
value, no parameters, no other codings; rejected together with
Content-Length.GET, HEAD, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE carry a body only with
http.allow_body_on_get: without it, Transfer-Encoding: chunked or a
Content-Length above zero on those methods is rejected
(body_on_bodiless_method), whatever the body turns out to hold. CONNECT
never carries a body.Expect may only be 100-continue; anything else gets 417. roxy sends
100 Continue once the rules allow the request; when a rule reads the
request body it goes out before the body is judged, and a deny follows
the body.On a listener with forwarded_for, X-Forwarded-For must name the
client at the trusted hop
(forwarded_for_invalid; clients behind a load balancer).Hop-by-hop fields (Connection and every field it names, Keep-Alive,
Proxy-Connection, Proxy-Authorization, Proxy-Authenticate, TE,
Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade) are consumed and never
forwarded.
Upgrade is honoured only for a WebSocket a rule allows.
92.title: Headers

93.text:
Chunk sizes are hex, at most 16 digits. Chunk extensions need
http.allow_chunk_extensions, and with them the whole chunk-size line is
at most 4096 bytes; trailers need http.allow_request_trailers
and an h2 origin (trailers). The final CRLF
is enforced.At most limits.max_request_body_bytes (1 GiB), enforced while
streaming: exceeding it closes the connection mid-stream.The first request head on a connection must arrive within
limits.header_timeout (10 s) of the connection opening; every later
head within header_timeout of its first byte, pipelined bytes included.
In a tunnel each step gets its own header_timeout: the CONNECT head,
the first bytes that say whether the tunnel carries TLS, the client TLS
handshake, then the first request head (on HTTP/2, the handshake and
then the first stream). The body may not stall longer than limits.body_idle_timeout (10 m), which also
bounds how long the client may go without taking the next part of the
response (on HTTP/2: stream reset with CANCEL, response_error, reason
client_stalled).A client that closes while roxy still waits for the response ends the
exchange; nothing is written back; reason client_gone.
93.title: Body

94.text:
Pseudo-headers (:method, :scheme, :authority, :path) exactly once
each, before regular headers.Connection-specific headers (connection, keep-alive,
transfer-encoding, upgrade, proxy-connection) reset the stream
(RFC 9113 §8.2.2). te is accepted only as trailers.:path goes through the same normaliser and limits.max_url_bytes cap
once the h2 crate has accepted it: a raw space, backtick, < or > in
:path resets the stream before roxy sees it, with no parse_error
event. :authority must equal the CONNECT authority; a host header, if
present, must equal :authority.limits.h2_max_concurrent_streams and limits.h2_max_header_list_bytes
cap streams per connection and header bytes per stream.
CONTINUATION-flood and rapid-reset defences come from the h2 crate.The first stream must open within limits.header_timeout; between
requests the connection may idle for limits.idle_timeout.
94.title: HTTP/2 requests

95.text:
Applied to the request target, for matching and forwarding alike. The path starts with / and contains pchar and /, with well-formed
percent-encodings. [ ] { } | ^ and ` are percent-encoded rather
than rejected (/a|b becomes /a%7Cb). Space, control bytes, ",
<, >, \ and non-ASCII are rejected.Percent-encoded unreserved characters (A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~) are
decoded; other encodings stay (%2F stays %2F).Hex digits in the remaining encodings are upper-cased.Dot segments (including ones %2E-encoded before step 2) are removed
per RFC 3986 §5.2.4. A path that climbs above the root is rejected.An empty path becomes /.The query is validated the same way and its hex upper-cased. /, ?,
[ and ] are also allowed raw; { } | ^ and ` are
percent-encoded; nothing is decoded. It is parsed into pairs for
matching only.A fragment in an HTTP/1.1 target is rejected. The h2 crate drops a
fragment from an HTTP/2 :path before roxy sees it.The host is lower-cased; IDNA labels must already be A-labels (xn--),
raw Unicode is rejected; the port is made explicit; a trailing dot is
removed.
95.title: URL normalisation

96.text:
HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1, whichever ALPN negotiates. HTTP/2 takes the
pseudo-headers from the canonical fields and drops host for
:authority. HTTP/1.1: METHOD <origin-form path[?query]> HTTP/1.1;host first, then the headers in canonical order, lowercase;content-length when known, otherwise clean chunked with no
extensions, never both; a body with trailers fails instead;connection management by roxy's pool; no client hop-by-hop field
survives. Changes from rules and addons are applied to the canonical model before
serialisation and pass the same validation: a header value with a CRLF
denies the flow.
96.title: Upstream serialisation

97.text:
Upstreams are trusted (threat model). hyper parses
the response and roxy builds a CanonicalResponse: Status and headers are kept, names lower-cased; Set-Cookie and
WWW-Authenticate stay separate fields.Hop-by-hop fields are stripped and the framing regenerated:
content-length when known, otherwise clean chunked (HTTP/1.1) or DATA
frames (HTTP/2), with the origin's trailers after the body
(trailers). Responses to HEAD, and 1xx,
204 and 304, carry no body. Empty non-final DATA frames are never
sent upstream.limits.max_response_body_bytes (1 GiB) caps the body.
limits.response_header_timeout (15 m) starts once the request body has
been sent; while it is still being sent, the exchange fails (504) only
if the upstream stops taking it for twice limits.body_idle_timeout.The upstream may pause up to limits.response_body_idle_timeout (30 m)
between parts of the body; longer ends the exchange (response_error,
reason response_body_timeout): close on HTTP/1.1, CANCEL on HTTP/2,
or a 504 while rules are still reading the body and nothing has been
sent.A client that closes while roxy waits for the next part of the body ends
the exchange at once on both versions: the body is dropped, releasing the
upstream and any service streams; a part already there is still written.
On HTTP/1.1 a client that shut down only its sending side counts as gone.Redirects are forwarded, not followed. Encoded bodies pass through
untouched (below).
97.title: Responses

98.text:
roxy decodes content-encoding to inspect a body, never to forward it:
body.text and response.body.text see the decoded text
(body rules); the bytes forwarded
are the bytes received. The one exception is addons: bodies are decoded at
the edge of the stack and forwarded decoded
(content codings for addons). codingformatgzip, x-gzipRFC 1952; several members in a row are one bodydeflatezlib format (RFC 1950), as RFC 9110 defines it; raw deflate is refusedbrRFC 7932, the window the stream declares (up to 16 MiB)zstdRFC 8878, window at most 8 MiB (RFC 9659) Stacked codings are undone in reverse order; identity is ignored; at
most 4 codings, more is refused.An empty body is empty whatever its coding.Decoding is strict: truncated data, a bad checksum, or bytes after the
end of the stream make the body undecodable.Decoders work in bounded steps (a highly compressed body costs time, not
memory); each decoder's window is charged to the
buffer budget before it is allocated.
The decoded size counts against the same cap as the body as sent. http.strip_accept_encoding (default false) removes accept-encoding from
every request as roxy reads it, so origins answer uncompressed. Addons,
rules and the flow log see the request without it.
98.title: Content codings

99.text:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
content-type: application/json
cache-control: no-store
x-roxy-rule: <rule id>
connection: close

{"error":"blocked by roxy","rule":"<rule id>","flow":"<flow id>"} Every refusal roxy originates has this body: refusalstatusrulea rule denies403, or the rule's deny.statusthe rule idthe process is quarantined403_quarantinedaddress floor403_address_policyunavailable policy input503_fail_closedfailed addon layer503layer:<name>upstream failure502 (504 for a timeout)none The body names the rule and the flow, never why: the reason code
(dns_failed, connect_failed, metric_table_full, ...) is in the flow
log only. A request roxy cannot parse is refused with a different body, before any
rule has seen it: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
content-type: application/json
connection: close

{"error":"rejected by roxy","reason":"cl_and_te"} reason is the parse_error code (rejection rules),
which describes the request's syntax and says nothing about policy. The
status is 400, or the closer one the code has (413, 414, 431, ...);
on HTTP/2 the stream is reset instead. A rule sets the status and message with deny: { status: 451, message:
"..." }. After a deny the connection is closed (connection: close on
HTTP/1.1, GOAWAY on HTTP/2) unless the rule says deny: { close: false
}. On HTTP/1.1 a kept-alive connection discards up to 1 MiB of the
refused body before the next request, and is closed instead beyond that; a
closing response lingers for up to 1 s, discarding up to 1 MiB, so the
client reads the response rather than a reset. After an upstream failure
(502, 504) the connection stays open on both versions.
99.title: Deny responses

100.text:
Every limit resolves in the closed direction: an error anywhere between
accept and the upstream connect produces a deny response or a closed socket
(fail closed).
100.title: Resource limits

101.text:
conditionresultthe process is quarantined403, _quarantined, close (quarantine)parse or canonicalisation errorclose the connection (400 if a response can still be written), parse_errora rule deniesdeny response, then closepolicy input unavailable (metric store, address list, secret)503, _fail_closedmetric key table full or byte budget exhausteddeny, metric_table_fullbody too large to inspect, as sent or decodeddeny, _fail_closed, body_too_large_to_inspectbody to inspect cannot be decodeddeny, _fail_closed, body_decode_failed or unsupported_content_encodingbody to sign over max_sign_body_bytes413, _sign, sign_body_too_largebuffer budget cannot cover the exchange's inspection, decoding, signing or WebSocket buffersdeny, _fail_closed, buffer_budget_exhausted; an observer's copy is cut instead (observer_lagged), an endpoint call refused, a body decoded for a layer failedbody or header limit exceeded mid-streamclose both sidesrequest trailers without http.allow_request_trailers, or a forbidden field in a trailer sectionrequest: 400 and close, or a stream reset, parse_error reason trailers; response: body cut, response_error (trailers)upstream DNS, connect or TLS failure502, upstream_errorupstream connect, TLS handshake or response-header timeout504, upstream_error, reason timeoutaddress floor403, _address_policyaddon trap, budget exceeded, invalid output, or no instance free within first_byte_timeout (enforce mode)deny, layer_error; observe-mode addons only logconfig reload failskeep the old policyconnection caprefuse the new connectionflow log or capture behind, or its disk failinghold traffic until it catches up; never drop recordsWebSocket message that breaks the protocol or is over max_ws_message_bytes, when rules read messagesclose both sides with 1002, 1007 or 1009 (WebSockets) The policy reason codes appear in the flow log only, never in the deny
response; a parse error's code is also in its 400 body
