(deny responses).
101.title: Fail-closed outcomes

102.text:
All under limits:; defaults shown. Sizes are 1024-based. limits:
  # client requests (HTTP)
  max_header_bytes: 64kb
  max_url_bytes: 8kb
  max_headers: 100
  max_request_body_bytes: 1gb
  header_timeout: 10s             # the slowloris guard: each step before a request head (CONNECT, TLS handshake, the head itself)
  body_idle_timeout: 10m          # the client's stall: sending its body, or taking the response
  idle_timeout: 1h                # keep-alive idle; also a relayed WebSocket's idle timeout
  h2_max_concurrent_streams: 100
  h2_max_header_list_bytes: 64kb

  # responses
  max_response_body_bytes: 1gb
  response_header_timeout: 15m    # from when the request body has been sent; a WebSocket upgrade's whole upstream handshake
  response_body_idle_timeout: 30m # the upstream's stall between parts of the response body

  # buffering
  max_inspect_body_bytes: 1mb     # body.text / response.body.text, and addons' default
  max_sign_body_bytes: 100mb      # a request body hashed for sign: aws_sigv4; larger is 413
  max_capture_body_bytes: 16mb    # per direction per exchange
  max_ws_message_bytes: 16mb      # a reassembled WebSocket message, when rules read ws.*
  max_observer_lag_bytes: 16mb    # how far behind an observe-mode addon may fall, per direction
  max_buffered_bytes: 1gb         # all of the above together, across the process

  # connections
  max_connections: 10000              # to the proxy listeners; ca_server has its own cap of the same size
  max_connections_per_client: 10000   # per client IP; omitted, it is max_connections, so off unless lowered

  # policy state
  max_metric_keys: 100000
  max_metric_bytes: 256mb         # at most 64gb
  max_state_entries: 100000
  max_address_list_bytes: 256mb limiton overrunbody_idle_timeoutthe request is cut (parse_error, body_timeout) or the response is cut (response_error; client_gone on HTTP/1.1, client_stalled on HTTP/2)response_body_idle_timeoutthe exchange ends (response_error, response_body_timeout): the connection closes on HTTP/1.1, the stream is reset with CANCEL on HTTP/2; while rules are still reading the body (response.body.text), nothing has been sent and the client gets a 504 insteadmax_ws_message_bytesboth sides close with 1009; applies only when rules read messages (WebSockets)max_observer_lag_bytesthe observer's copy is cut (addon modes) The upstream dial is timed by upstream.connect_timeout (10 s), not a
limits key: once for the TCP connect over all of a name's addresses and
once more for the TLS handshake, so an upstream that accepts the connection
but never completes TLS is cut after a second connect_timeout (504,
upstream_error, reason timeout, message upstream TLS handshake;
upstream). Addons have their own limits, and fixed caps on what the host holds for a
guest (addon limits).
102.title: Limits

103.text:
The timeouts are permissive by default: roxy decides what passes, not how
long a well-behaved exchange may take, and a model call with minutes to its
first byte, a quiet WebSocket or a stream with long gaps should not hit one
unless the operator chose it. Only header_timeout is tight. Memory is
bounded by the buffer budget and the per-connection caps, not by the
timeouts, so a long timeout costs only the idle connection it keeps: timeouta long value holdsheader_timeouta connection slot (one of max_connections, or of the ca_server cap) and its socket, with no request to show for itbody_idle_timeouta connection slot and the exchange's buffers (its reservations under max_buffered_bytes, and up to 4 MiB of HTTP/2 receive window) while the client is silentidle_timeouta connection slot and its socket between requests, or a relayed WebSocket's two sockets and its reserved message buffers while nothing is sentresponse_header_timeouta connection slot, the upstream connection, and the exchange's buffers while the upstream thinksresponse_body_idle_timeoutthe same as above while the upstream pauses mid-body Tightening one trades those idle connections for cut exchanges; raise
max_connections instead if idle connections are what runs out. An upstream may return its response before consuming the whole upload.
The response can reach the client immediately, but the final flow record
waits until upload accounting finishes. After that response head, roxy
checks upload progress every twice body_idle_timeout. If no bytes were
consumed during an interval, roxy cancels the remaining upload and records
upstream_body_timeout, unless another failure already supplies the reason.
This check runs while response rules and response writing are still in
progress, including exchanges without addon layers.
The timeout measures bytes consumed from the forwarded body, not which
participant caused the delay. It also covers an addon holding the upload
or an HTTP/1.1 response rule waiting while the client socket is not being
pumped. It can therefore accompany a successful response status.
A client cancellation also cancels the upload and releases its buffers.
103.title: Timeouts

104.text:
max_buffered_bytes bounds inspection and copy payloads in aggregate.
An exchange reserves before it fills a charged buffer; a reservation the
budget cannot cover fails at once, with no waiting and no eviction (503,
_fail_closed, buffer_budget_exhausted). This is the whole list of what
is charged: bufferreservationa body a rule reads (body.text, response.body.text)max_inspect_body_bytes, or its content-length if smaller; a body with a content-encoding reserves the whole cap, whatever its length, since its decoded size is not known until it is; nothing for a body known to be empty (no request body, a HEAD response, a 1xx, 204 or 304). Once buffered, it shrinks to what is held (the body as sent with its trailers, or its decoded text if larger) and stays until the exchange ends. A body over the cap holds only what was read before that was known: nothing when its content-length said so, the prefix read when it was found out mid-streama content decodereach decoder's window, charged before the decoder is created: 32 KiB for gzip or deflate, the window a br stream's first byte declares (1 KiB to 16 MiB), 8 MiB for zstd (the largest window accepted, which each frame may use). Stacked codings add up. Held while the decoder runs: for the rule's decision on an inspected body, for the whole body when it is decoded for the addon stack (http.decode_for_addons). A window the budget cannot cover fails closed before it is allocateda request body hashed for sign: aws_sigv4its content-length (at most max_sign_body_bytes) up front; a chunked body reserves chunk by chunk up to that cap and is refused at the chunk the budget cannot cover. Held until the exchange ends. unsigned_payload: true reserves nothing (signing AWS requests)an endpoint call's request bodywhat the guest sends, frame by frame as it is read (at most 16 MiB), held until the call is answered. A body the budget cannot cover refuses the call (host services)a WebSocket whose messages rules readtwice max_ws_message_bytes at the upgrade, held for the session. Reading bodies but not messages holds nothing for a WebSocketan observer's copythe bytes queued and not yet read, frame by frame, given back as the observer reads them (or drops the copy). A copy whose next frame would overrun the budget is cut (observer_lagged, reason: buffer_budget_exhausted): the budget bounds how far behind observers are in total, not how many exchanges are observed. A copy whose observer gets no instance within its first_byte_timeout is dropped the same way (reason: no_instance), so a busy observer cannot pin budget that enforce flows need Streaming buffers have separate bounds and are outside this budget:
HTTP/2 receive windows (connections), codec
parse buffers, depth-two lane channels, WASM output queues (two 64 KiB
frames), and service layer feeder staging.
A service input can retain two queued lane frames plus its 256 KiB credit
window; with 256 KiB frames that is 768 KiB of unread payload per body.
Credit returns when the feeder enqueues a frame, before the final consumer
reads it. In the other direction, each blocked pump retains one source
frame and shares a 64-message socket queue; body messages are at most
64 KiB each. These bounds scale with live streams and layers. Socket buffers,
metadata, allocation overhead, guest memory and external service memory
are additional: max_buffered_bytes is not a process RAM ceiling. While reclaiming an HTTP/1.1 exchange, further reads stop at
max_header_bytes, plus one byte to observe EOF at the boundary; existing
codec read-ahead is retained too. This watch also runs while an unread
upload fills its body queue. Once the read-ahead buffer is full,
the upload consumer must make room or the exchange must finish within
header_timeout, otherwise the connection closes;
queued bytes cannot disable cancellation indefinitely. Ordinary pipelined
requests remain buffered until the preceding exchange releases its work. Backpressure still obeys timeout policy. HTTP/1.1 bounds a stalled request
consumer by body_idle_timeout; HTTP/2 arms its request input-idle timer
when a consumer waits for data. An approval addon holding an unread upload
can therefore reach the HTTP/1.1 deadline even while sending keepalives.
After the upstream head, the upload-progress deadline described above
applies to both transports. Budget ÷ cap is how many exchanges can hold a buffer at once (defaults:
1024 bodies of unknown length under inspection, 32 WebSockets with message
rules, 1 GiB of unread observer copy). It must be at least the largest
single reservation.
104.title: Buffer budget

105.text: settingtakes effectmax_header_bytes, max_url_bytes, max_headers, max_request_body_bytes, header_timeout, body_idle_timeout, response_body_idle_timeout, idle_timeout, the h2_* limits, the http.* flagsfixed when a connection is accepted; new connections only. A relayed WebSocket takes idle_timeout from its exchange's snapshot insteadmax_inspect_body_bytes, max_sign_body_bytes, max_response_body_bytes, response_header_timeout, the WebSocket limits, max_observer_lag_bytes, the policy itselfper exchange, from the snapshot the exchange starts under, on old connections toomax_buffered_bytesprocess-wide: each reservation is checked against the value in force at that moment; reservations already held stay as they are
105.title: Reload

106.text:
A connection over max_connections or max_connections_per_client is
accepted and closed at once, with a connection_refused event. The
per-client cap counts TCP peers: it is applied when the connection is
accepted, before any X-Forwarded-For is read, so a listener's
forwarded_for does not change what it counts. The ca_server listener counts separately, max_connections in
total with no per-client cap, and logs its refusals to roxy's own log
rather than the flow log. A client that fills it starves the health
probes, so that port should not be reachable by untrusted clients.Every read is bounded (head size, body size, ClientHello size) and every
stage has a timeout. Nothing is allocated in proportion to an
attacker-supplied number before it is validated (content-length: 10^18
does not pre-allocate).Request bytes in flight on an HTTP/2 connection (sent by the client, not
yet taken by the upstream) sit outside max_buffered_bytes: the
connection's receive window caps them at 4 MiB, so one client IP can hold
at most max_connections_per_client × 4 MiB. Omitted, it is whatever
max_connections is, so behind a load balancer (one source IP for every
client, whatever forwarded_for resolves) the cap is the fleet's; lower
it on a proxy port where each client has its own address.Upstream connections are bounded by the clients: HTTP/1.1 origins get
one connection per concurrent request, HTTP/2 origins at most
upstream.max_h2_connections_per_origin (4 by default), each with an
8 MiB receive window (upstream).Bounded policy tables (metrics, state) never evict
(never evict).The proxy port serves only proxy semantics and roxy.internal; health
and CA download live on the separate ca_server listener, with a cap of
its own, so the two hold at most 2 × max_connections connection slots
between them.A panic in a connection task closes that connection only.On SIGTERM or Ctrl-C roxy stops accepting, drains exchanges in flight
for up to 10 seconds, and flushes the flow log and capture before
exiting.
106.title: Connections

107.text:
Metrics count exchanges or bytes over a sliding window; state is a bounded
key/value store written with set_state and read as state["key"].
107.title: Rate limits and state

108.text:
Defined once, compared in rules (metric.<id> >= 30). metrics:
  - id: <string>
    count: requests | request_bytes | response_bytes | errors | denied | unique(<field>)
    where: <expr>        # admission values only, no tags: whether it counts
    key: [<field>, ...]  # scalar admission fields; omitted = one global series
    window: <duration>   # omitted = cumulative since start; 0 is a compile error
    max_keys: <n>        # series this metric alone may hold; omitted = limits.max_metric_keys Windows slide in 60 fixed buckets (1-second resolution for 1m). The
store keeps 60 complete buckets plus the current partial one, so a value
may include events up to one bucket older than the window: a limit trips
slightly early, never late. unique is a HyperLogLog sketch per bucket.where may read admission fields, header[..], query[..],
state[..], body.text and metrics; not tag[..] (counted outside the
rules, a tag would always read false). key and the unique(..)
field take scalar admission fields only (client.ip, host, tls.sni, ...),
not header[..] or other indexed values. Anything else is a compile
error.Nullable keys. A flow whose key field is null is denied
(_fail_closed). A key or unique(..) field nullable on an ordinary flow
(tls.sni, tls.alpn, tls.version on plaintext; query.raw without a
query; body.size when chunked) must be guarded in where (tls.sni !=
null, or an and with that as a top-level term) or the metric does not
compile; such flows are not counted. A rule reading the metric needs the
same guard (tls.sni != null and metric.by_sni > 30).When counts move. requests and denied are read before the
forwarding decision and incremented after it (denied flows count), so
metric.x >= 30 denies the 31st request. request_bytes and
response_bytes grow as bytes stream: a deny or quarantine reading them
is re-checked in flight and stops the exchange that crosses the limit; a
chunk is counted before it is checked, so a budget overcounts by at most
one chunk. errors count when the exchange ends.Bounds (never evict):
limits.max_metric_keys (100 000) series across all metrics; each
metric's max_keys (at most the shared limit, its default); and,
approximately, limits.max_metric_bytes (256 MiB, at most 64 GiB; a
series is charged for key, buckets and a fixed overhead). A flow needing
a new series when any is exhausted is denied (_fail_closed, reason
metric_table_full); a byte metric that cannot record a chunk mid-stream
stops the exchange the same way. Series are reclaimed only once their
window has fully expired.Reload. A metric keeps its series when its id, count, where,
key and window are unchanged (where compared as written); any other
change to it starts it empty, and a removed metric's series are dropped
silently. Changing only max_keys carries over. Carried series may
exceed a lowered max_metric_keys or max_keys until they expire (new
series refused meanwhile), but never the byte budget: a series that does
not fit is dropped with a warning.
108.title: Metrics

109.text:
host, path, url and query.raw are chosen by the client per
request, and denied flows count, so a metric keyed on one with
no where fills with as many series as the client sends, without one
request being allowed; then every flow needing a new series is denied
(metric_table_full) until series expire. Bound the key with a finite
where: metrics:
  - id: github_requests
    count: requests
    where: host in ["api.github.com", "github.com"]
    key: [host]
    window: 1m client.ip is bounded by who can reach the proxy; behind a load balancer
it is each client's own address only with the listener's forwarded_for
(HTTP). roxy check warns when a
metric keys on any of the four fields above with no where. host under
"github.com" does not bound host: subdomains are client-chosen too. For
path, url and query.raw a where on host limits
whose values count, not how many; give such a metric a where that
enumerates the values it keys on, or its own max_keys so filling it
refuses new series in that metric alone. unique(..) fields are not keys:
they feed a bounded sketch inside a series and create none.
109.title: Key cardinality

110.text:
A bounded key/value map with per-entry TTL: the rule's ttl, or one hour;
ttl: 0 is a compile error. At most limits.max_state_entries (100 000)
stored entries, expired ones included until they are purged (every 1024
writes, and at most every 100 ms when a new key meets a full table); a new
key when full denies the flow (503, _fail_closed, reason
state_unavailable). State is shared across flows, so reads are
order-dependent: state["key"] sees what earlier flows wrote and, within
a flow, the set_state of rules above the reader. A WASM layer reads and
writes the same store (host services).
110.title: State

111.text:
The protocol between a roxy node (a roxy process in node mode) and its
control plane (any server implementing these four operations). The contract
is
spec/node-protocol/v1/openapi.yaml:
the example bodies here are checked against its schemas in CI and titled
with the schema each satisfies. A node enrols once with a bootstrap token and receives a node token, then
authenticates with it to poll for its lease, ship its flow log and renew
the token. The lease is the whole policy: a rendered roxy.yaml, the
secret values it names, and how long it is good for. An expired lease
denies everything. The control plane never pushes; the node polls.
111.title: Node protocol

112.text:
HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TLS; all paths start with /roxy/v1/. Bodies
are JSON, Content-Type: application/json; unknown fields are ignored by
both sides. The node's User-Agent is roxy/<roxy_version>.Every request carries Authorization: Bearer <token>: the enrolment
token at enrolment, the node token everywhere else. The node presents no
client certificate, so the control plane can sit behind any TLS
terminator; a token only ever travels inside the server's TLS. A request
other than enrolment whose token the server does not recognise is
answered 401.Bootstrap material, given out of band: the control plane URL, an
enrolment token, and optionally a PEM bundle of CA certificates to verify
the control plane with (otherwise the system roots).
112.title: Transport

113.text:
Every non-2xx response carries an error body: error is a stable code,
message is for humans, and a 426 adds missing
(unsupported versions). A
node acts on the status code, not the body. {"error": "invalid_token", "message": "enrolment token not recognised"} statusmeaningnode behaviour400malformed request; error says howlogged apart from a 401; retrying cannot help. Enrolment: retry with backoff for two minutes, then exit non-zero. Renewal: stop renewing. Lease: log once per outcome change, keep polling and let the lease run down. A flow batch is the exception (flow upload)401at enrolment: the token was not accepted. Elsewhere: the node token is not recognised (never issued, expired or forgotten)enrolment: retry with backoff for two minutes (a new token may not have reached every replica), then exit non-zero. Renewal: log once per run of them and retry with backoff under the current token (the replica answering may not yet know the token the last renewal issued). Lease: log once per outcome change, keep polling and let the lease run down. Flows: retry the batch with backoff, as a failure. Never re-enrol unasked: re-enrolment is an operator action410the node is revoked; definite and terminalat enrolment: exit non-zero at once. Elsewhere: expire the lease at once (deny everything, clear the secrets), stop polling, keep /healthz up and /readyz not ready, and offer what is spooled to /flows for up to thirty seconds426the server will not serve this node's protocol_version or roxy_versionenrolment: exit non-zero at once. Renewal: stop renewing. Lease: treat as 5xx; log the missing list distinctly507flow quota exhaustedstop shipping until a lease with a new lease_id arrives (flow upload)5xx, timeout, connection or TLS errorthe control plane is unavailableretry with backoff; the lease runs down
113.title: Errors

114.title: Enrol

115.text:
POST /roxy/v1/renew with the node token and the enrol body; the response
has the enrolment response's shape, with node_id unchanged and a fresh
token. The server keeps accepting the old token until its own
not_after, so a renewal that has reached one replica but not another
cannot lock the node out; the node switches to the new token on receipt
and replaces the one in its state directory. 5xx, timeout, connection and TLS errors are retried with backoff, and so
is a 401: the replica answering may not yet know the token the last
renewal issued, so the node keeps trying under the token it has, logging
once per run of them. 410 is terminal; a 426 or other 4xx is logged
once and ends renewal, and the token serves until its not_after. Once it
expires the node exits non-zero with an error naming the remedy (a new
enrolment token and an empty state dir), as it does on a start whose
stored token has already
expired: no control plane recognises the token, so nothing short of
re-enrolment recovers the node.
115.title: Renew

116.title: Lease

117.text:
{
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "valid_for_seconds": 900,
  "refresh_after_seconds": 300,
  "config": "version: 1\nlisteners:\n  - name: proxy\n    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080\nsecrets:\n  github: { lease: true }\nrules:\n  - id: github\n    when: host == \"api.github.com\"\n    then: [allow]\n",
  "secrets": {
    "github": "ghp_example"
  },
  "state_epoch": "2026-10-06T09:00:00Z",
  "flow": {
    "ship": true,
    "batch_max_bytes": 1048576,
    "flush_interval_seconds": 5,
    "spool_high_water_bytes": 67108864,
    "on_high_water": "hold"
  },
  "quarantine": {
    "release": ["q-01J9ZB7QX4R2M8K3N5P6T7V8W9"]
  }
} fieldmeaninglease_idopaque; changes whenever any other field changes. The node reports it on every poll and quotes it in flow batchesvalid_for_secondsa duration, not an instant: the node sets valid_until = sent_at + valid_for_seconds from its own clock, sent_at being just before it sent the request, so a slow answer shortens the lease and clock skew has no effect. The server's clock is never usedrefresh_after_secondswhen to poll next, counted the same way; leave room for several retries before valid_for_seconds runs out (a third of it is reasonable). The node never polls later than halfway through the leaseconfiga complete roxy.yaml as a string, with no secret values: every secrets: entry the lease supplies is name: { lease: true }secretseach secret name the config declares, to its value, a UTF-8 string. The node reads a missing map as empty, which refuses the lease if the config declares any lease: true secretstate_epochopaque. When it differs from the previous lease's, the node clears every rule set_state entry and every metric window before applying the lease (how a control plane lifts a lockout a rule imposed with set_state); unchanged, state survives a config change. The first lease sets it without clearing anythingflowflow upload settings. ship: false turns shipping off; the other fields are still required. on_high_water is hold (apply roxy's backpressure to traffic when the spool is full) or spool (drop the oldest spooled events, logging once)quarantinereleases of the node's quarantine. release lists incident ids the control plane has released; the node lifts its quarantine when the quarantine.id it reports is among them, and ignores any other id, so a release decided before a later trip lifts nothing. Ids may stay listed indefinitely. Orthogonal to the policy: the rest of the lease is applied whether or not the node is quarantined, so the policy is current the moment the quarantine lifts. Optional; a server that has released nothing leaves it outinterception_careserved; a v1 server does not send it and a v1 node ignores it (the node accepts any value here, whatever the schema says) The node applies only what differs from what it holds: a changed config
rebuilds the policy (the atomic snapshot swap of a file reload); changed
secrets alone swap the in-memory secret map and update the redactor,
leaving rules, addons and upstream pools alone; neither changed only moves
valid_until. A lease is applied in full or not at all: a config that
roxy check would reject, or a secrets map missing a name the config
declares, is logged and discarded, and the node keeps the lease it has. A
node without a lease denies everything and reports not ready.
117.title: Lease body

118.text:
A node reports protocol_version and roxy_version at enrolment, renewal
and every lease fetch. A server that does not speak the protocol version,
or will not serve nodes below some roxy release, answers 426 naming what
the node lacks: {"error": "unsupported", "message": "roxy 0.1.0 is below this server's floor of 0.2.0", "missing": ["roxy_version:0.2.0"]} There is no other capability negotiation: the node parses config
strictly, so a lease using something it does not understand fails to load,
and the lease_id on its next poll shows the server it was not applied.
118.title: Unsupported versions

119.text:
POST /roxy/v1/flows with the node token. The body may be gzip
compressed, signalled with Content-Encoding: gzip. {
  "node_id": "node-7f3a9c",
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "seq_first": 1042,
  "events": [
    {"seq": 1042, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.123Z", "event": "request", "flow": "01J9Z8", "decision": "deny", "terminal_rule": "_default"},
    {"seq": 1043, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.410Z", "event": "log", "flow": "01J9Z9", "rule": "audit"}
  ]
} fieldmeaningnode_idmust match the node the token names, or the answer is 400 node_mismatchlease_idthe lease in force when the batch was assembled; any lease id issued to the node is acceptedseq_firstthe seq of the first event; events are consecutive and in order from it, or the server answers 400eventsflow log records with seq added: a per-node counter that increases by one per shipped event, persisted in the state directory in blocks so it keeps increasing across restarts (a restart skips to the end of the last reservation, at most two blocks of 1024) A batch is at most the lease's batch_max_bytes (the JSON before
compression); the node flushes when that is reached or
flush_interval_seconds has passed since the first unsent event. A server
that refuses a batch within the size it stated is treated as 5xx. {"acked_through": 1043} Delivery is at least once: the server stores the batch, deduplicating on
(node_id, seq), and answers 200 with the highest seq it has stored
for the node; the node drops spooled events at or below acked_through. A
gap within one run means events were dropped (spool mode at the high
water): a server-side alert, not a protocol error. Restarts and ship:
false also leave gaps. responsenode behaviour400 (node_mismatch, a lease_id the server never issued, events not consecutive)logged apart from an outage; the batch is unshipped audit and stays spooled, so under hold traffic stalls until the control plane accepts it507log once and apply on_high_water to what accumulates until a new lease arrives; the control plane is expected to revoke the node or issue it a new lease410shipping stops, and so does the drain that follows a 410 on the lease: a control plane that wants a revoked node's last events keeps accepting its batches401, 5xxas in the errors table
119.title: Flow upload

120.text:
The when / where expression language and the actions of then.
Evaluation is in policy evaluation.
120.title: Rule language

121.text:
Statically typed; no user-defined functions; linear-time matching (regex
crate, no backtracking). expr        := or
or          := and ( "or" and )*
and         := not ( "and" not )*
not         := "not" not | primary
primary     := "(" expr ")" | comparison | predicate
comparison  := operand OP operand
predicate   := field | bool                  ; boolean field, or a literal (`where: true`)
operand     := field | field "[" string "]" | literal
OP          := "==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">="
             | "in" | "not in"
             | "starts_with" | "ends_with" | "contains"
             | "like"        ; glob, full match ( * ? )
             | "matches"     ; regex, full match
             | "under"       ; host == X or host ends_with "." + X
literal     := string | number [unit] | bool | list | ip | cidr | @list | method | "null"
list        := "[" literal ("," literal)* "]"
unit        := kb | mb | gb | ms | s | m | h      ; sizes are 1024-based
method      := [A-Z][A-Z_]*                       ; HTTP method names only A rule without when matches every exchange; a metric without where
counts every one.Strings: double-quoted, \" and \\ escapes. # ... comments are
allowed in multi-line YAML block scalars.Comparison is byte-exact, except: host, tls.sni and scheme operands
compare ASCII case-insensitively under every operator (like, matches,
in included); under is case-insensitive whatever its left operand;
header["X-Y"] names are case-insensitive, values not. A header value
with obs-text (bytes 0x80 and up, under http.allow_obs_text) reads as
one character per byte (ISO-8859-1), so the text a rule matches is the
bytes roxy forwards: the byte 0xE9 reads as é, while é sent in
UTF-8 (0xC3 0xA9) reads as the two characters Ã©. method is
exact: method get is forwarded as an extension method, may carry a
body, and matches neither method == GET nor method in [GET, HEAD].Compile errors: type mismatch (host under 443), a regex that does not
compile, a like pattern longer than 1 KiB, a bad CIDR mask, metric.foo with no such metric, an undefined
@list, a ${secret:name} placeholder in a string (it would compare
against its own text; secrets), and a predicate
that can never match: under with an empty label ("a..b",
"example.com.."), a host or tls.sni literal with a trailing dot
(host == "evil.example.", host like "*.example.com."), non-ASCII
characters, brackets ("[::1]") or an IPv4-mapped address
("::ffff:10.0.0.1") (fields),
or null compared with a value that is never null
(missing values). in
takes a list of the operand's type, a CIDR, or an @list for ip fields.
121.title: Expressions

122.text:
Admission fields are known at the forwarding decision; a rule reading only
them is an admission rule. In-flight fields become known or change after the
request is forwarded; a rule reading one is re-checked in flight
(evaluation). fieldtypeknownclient.ipipadmissionlistener.namestringadmissiontls.sni, tls.alpn, tls.versionstringadmissionmethod, scheme, host, port, path, urlstring / intadmissionquery["k"], query.rawstringadmissionheader["name"], header.all["name"]string, listadmissionbody.sizeint: declared length, null if undeclared (chunked)admissionbody.textstring: the buffered body, up to the capadmissionmetric.<id>intadmission; a deny or quarantine reading a byte metric is also re-checked in flight (rate limits)state["key"], tag["name"]string, booladmissionbody.bytesint: request body bytes so farin-flightresponse.status, response.header["name"], response.header.all["name"]int, string, listin-flightresponse.body.sizeint: declared length, null if undeclaredin-flightresponse.body.textstring: the buffered response bodyin-flightresponse.body.bytesint: response body bytes so farin-flightws.direction, ws.opcode, ws.size, ws.textstring, int, int, string: the WebSocket message being checkedin-flight, per message (WebSockets) client.ip is the client as roxy establishes it: the TCP peer, or on a
listener with forwarded_for the client X-Forwarded-For names at the
trusted hop (HTTP).
Either way it is canonical: an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (::ffff:10.0.0.1,
how an IPv4 client reaches a dual-stack [::] listener) is the IPv4 address
it embeds, so client.ip == 10.0.0.1 matches it.
path is normalised (HTTP). host
and tls.sni are the name as roxy delivers it: lower-case, without a
trailing dot, internationalised labels in A-label (xn--) form, and an IP
literal as the bare address (10.0.0.1, ::1; never [::1]), with an
IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal ([::ffff:10.0.0.1]) delivered as the IPv4 address
it embeds, since that is what gets dialled. A string literal compared with
them in another form never matches and is a compile error. Any rule reading ws.* makes roxy decode every WebSocket message
and strip WebSocket extensions. The normalised path is what roxy forwards, but an upstream may change it
again before resolving it: decode %2F to /, merge empty segments
(//admin), strip ;params, or fold case. A deny keyed on a path prefix
is therefore fragile: /a/..%2Fsecret does not start with /secret, yet an
upstream that decodes %2F first serves /a/../secret. An allow keyed on
a prefix has the same gap. Allow exact paths, or a prefix together with a
guard against every form the upstream reinterprets, raw or encoded
(not path contains "%2F", likewise "%5C", "//", ";" and "%3B"; hex
is upper-cased before matching, so one case suffices), and treat a path
deny as defence in depth
(URL normalisation).
122.title: Fields

123.text:
An absent value is null: an unsent header or query parameter, an unset
state key, tls.sni when none was sent, body.size for a chunked body.
tag["x"] is never null (false until set), nor are metric.<id>,
body.text and response.body.text (unavailable, they fail closed);
comparing any of them with null is a compile error. ==, !=, in and
not in treat null as a value; any other operator on it fails closed. expression, with x missingresultx == nulltruex != nullfalsex == "a", x in [...]falsex != "a", x not in [...]truex > 10, x contains "a", x matches "...", x under "...", x in 10.0.0.0/8, x in @listfails closed: _fail_closed, reason missing_value, naming the field and and or short-circuit, and a failure in any branch they reach is
final: body.size != null and body.size > 10mb is safe, body.size > 1 or
true on a chunked body fails closed, so the null test goes first in an
or as well (body.size == null or body.size > 1). null may appear only
in x == null / x != null. A metric keyed on a nullable field
needs the same guard in its where (rate limits).
123.title: Missing values (null)

124.text:
then is required: one action, or a list with at most one terminal action
(allow, deny or quarantine), last. An action is a bare word or a single-key map of
name to argument; a multi-key map, an unknown action, a wrong-shaped
argument or anything after a terminal action is a compile error. then: allow
then: { deny: { status: 451, message: "no" } }
then:
  - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
  - remove_header: [x-debug]
  - tag: billing
  - allow: { upgrade: websocket } Terminal: actionwhereeffectallowadmission rulesForward. upgrade: websocket permits a WebSocket upgrade; private_ok: true lets the flow reach private addresses (address floor).denyall rulesdeny: { status, message, close }; status 403 by default, 4xx or 5xx. At admission: refuse (deny responses) and close unless close: false. In flight: stop the exchange (evaluation). On a WebSocket: close both sides, with a 1008 frame when rules read messages (WebSockets).quarantineall rulesA bare word, no argument. A deny with status 403 that closes, plus: the whole proxy is quarantined, refusing every later exchange until released from outside. Any matching quarantine trips it, whichever deny decided the exchange, a fail-closed included. Needs --state-dir. Non-terminal: actionwhereeffectset_header: { name: value }request: admission rules; response: in-flight rulesSet or replace. Request values may use ${secret:name}; an invalid value denies the flow. A response rule may read only values known before the response head is sent (response.status, response.header[..], response.body.size, response.body.text); body.bytes, response.body.bytes, ws.* or a byte metric is a compile error.remove_header: [names]as set_headerrewrite_path: { match, to }admission rulesAnchored regex (as matches), $1 / ${name} groups; to must start with /; result re-normalised.set_query: { k: v }, remove_query: [k]admission rulesredirect: { host, port, scheme?, rewrite_host? }admission rulesChange the upstream target. host: DNS name, dotted-quad IPv4 or bracketed IPv6 ([::1]); anything else, or port 0, is a config error. The new IPs pass the address floor and deny lists. Host is unchanged unless rewrite_host: true, and while unchanged the request goes upstream over HTTP/1.1 (HTTP/2 needs :authority and host to agree).tag: nameallSets tag["name"] for later rules, addons and the log.log: { level, message }allEmits a log flow event.set_state: { key, value, ttl? }allWrites the state store.capture: request | response | bothadmission rulesTees the exchange, as forwarded, to the capture log.digest: request | response | bothadmission rulesHashes the selected bodies, as forwarded, into the flow record's body_sha256. Nothing is hashed without it.sign: { aws_sigv4: { service, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key, session_token?, unsigned_payload? } }admission rulesAWS Signature Version 4 over the forwarded request, after every other admission effect (signing AWS requests). Anything richer is an addon. call and passthrough are rejected with a
reason naming why.
124.title: Actions

125.text:
body.text and response.body.text are the only fields that buffer. If
any rule reads body.text, roxy collects every request body up to
limits.max_inspect_body_bytes (1 MiB) before the admission decision, then
streams it on; response.body.text likewise for every response body. A
body over the cap is unavailable: a rule reading it fails closed
(_fail_closed, reason body_too_large_to_inspect). Raise the cap, or
scope the rule (body.size != null and body.size < 1mb and ...) so it
short-circuits before the text; that avoids the fail-closed, not the
buffering. No body rule, no buffering. The text is the body decoded by its content-encoding
(content codings), as lossy UTF-8; the
forwarded bytes are the bytes received. The cap applies to the decoded text
too. An undecodable body fails closed: body_decode_failed (corrupt,
truncated, or bytes after the end of the stream) or
unsupported_content_encoding.
125.title: Body rules

126.text:
secrets: maps names to sources. ${secret:name} in an admission rule's
set_header value or sign credentials, or an addon endpoint's headers,
injects the value; the client holds only a placeholder. A reference
anywhere else is a compile error. secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline (`\n` or `\r\n`) stripped; warns if group or world can read it
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control-plane lease

rules:
  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # replaces whatever the client sent
      - allow Exactly one of env, file, lease: true; {}, null, a bare word
and lease: false are parse errors.env and file resolve at start and on reload; missing or empty is
fatal. roxy check and roxy rule test do not resolve secrets.At evaluation, a missing secret fails closed (_fail_closed, reason
secret_missing); one that is not a valid header value, secret_invalid.Injected values are redacted from the flow log and capture heads.A redirect in a matching rule sends the request, injected values
included, to the redirect target: a secret's set_header rule should
not match a request another rule redirects elsewhere.
126.title: Secrets

127.text:
sign: { aws_sigv4: ... }, an admission-rule action, signs the forwarded request
with AWS Signature Version 4, so a client holding placeholder credentials
reaches AWS with a real signature. Credential fields take ${secret:name} as
set_header does; session_token is optional. secrets:
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }
  aws_token: { env: AWS_SESSION_TOKEN }

rules:
  - id: bedrock
    when: host under "bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com" and scheme == "https"
    then:
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
            session_token: "${secret:aws_token}"   # optional
      - allow Signed: the request as forwarded, after every other admission effect
(set_header, rewrite_path, redirect, ...) whatever sign's
position in then. The client's authorization, x-amz-date,
x-amz-security-token and x-amz-content-sha256 are removed first.
host is signed as sent upstream. Not signed: connection,
transfer-encoding, content-length, accept-encoding, te,
trailer, upgrade, keep-alive, proxy-connection (re-serialised by
roxy), user-agent, x-amzn-trace-id (changed by intermediaries).
Every other header is. A non-UTF-8 header value (obs-text, under
http.allow_obs_text) is refused with 400 (terminal_rule: _sign,
reason: sign_header_invalid).service is the signing name (bedrock, s3, execute-api, ...).
s3, s3-control and s3-outposts use the S3 variant: path encoded
once, not normalised; payload hash sent as x-amz-content-sha256.Presigned: a request whose query carries X-Amz-Signature goes out
under the client's query signature, its authorization and x-amz-*
signature headers stripped, no signature of roxy's; mutations records
sign:presigned. It reaches AWS as whoever signed the URL; the rule's
host and path conditions bound where it may go.Two matching rules that both sign fail closed (sign_conflict).Body: buffered up to limits.max_sign_body_bytes (100 MiB) for the
payload hash; over that, declared or chunked, is 413 (terminal_rule:
_sign, reason: sign_body_too_large) and the connection closed.
unsigned_payload: true signs UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD and streams the body;
only S3 accepts it, so it is a config error with any other service.Tools: mutations records sign:aws_sigv4; the credentials are
redacted like any secret. roxy rule test shows sign aws_sigv4
service=... region=... without computing a signature; roxy check
validates the block.
127.title: Signing AWS requests

128.text:
name: { lease: true } declares a secret the control plane supplies in
memory with the lease (node protocol).
roxy check accepts it; standalone roxy run --config refuses to start,
naming the secret. Values live in a store beside the compiled policy. Replacing the map swaps
the store and rebuilds the redactor without recompiling rules, rebuilding
addons, flushing upstream pools or a reload event. An exchange resolves
every name, in its rules and in the headers of the endpoint calls its
addons make, from the generation current at its admission evaluation, so a swap
mid-evaluation cannot pair one credential with another's replacement; an
exchange under way keeps the generation it injected, and redacts with it,
however many swaps follow. A name the map lacks is secret_missing. Values
never appear in the config file, on disk or in logs. A config reload
resolves env and file sources into the same store.
128.title: Lease secrets

129.text:
How roxy speaks TLS to clients. The CA itself is in
managing the CA.
129.title: TLS

130.text:
Minted on demand per host: a DNS SAN, or an IP SAN for IP targets; ECDSA
P-256; 7-day validity, or until the CA expires if sooner; signed by the CA;
all leaves share one key pair. Cached in an LRU of tls.leaf_cache_size
entries (at least 1; roxy check refuses 0), minted on the blocking pool
for the name the handshake will serve (the SNI, or the CONNECT host when
the client sends none).
130.title: Leaf certificates

131.text:
The certificate is picked by SNI; no SNI means the CONNECT host. An SNI
that is present but invalid fails the handshake. Valid means valid as a
request host: ASCII A-labels, IPv6 in brackets, and a last label that is
numeric or 0x-hex only as a dotted-quad IPv4 address.Hosts are canonicalised everywhere (lower-cased, one trailing dot
removed), and that form is the leaf cache key: CONNECT Example.COM.:443
with SNI example.com is one host and one leaf.ALPN offers h2 (with http.enable_h2) and http/1.1.TLS 1.2 and 1.3. No session resumption: no session storage, no TLS 1.3
tickets.The handshake must complete within limits.header_timeout
(tls_handshake_timeout).
131.title: Client-facing TLS

132.text:
After a CONNECT, roxy reads just enough of the first TLS record to confirm
the tunnel carries TLS and extract the SNI and ALPN, with a hard cap
(16 KiB) and a timeout. The whole handshake message must be present and
well-formed. A ClientHello split across several TLS records, or a malformed
server_name (non-ASCII, control characters, NUL, duplicate entries), counts as not TLS and the connection is closed.
132.title: ClientHello sniffing

133.text:
How roxy reaches the origin: its own DNS, the
address floor that every
connection passes, and upstream TLS. upstream:
  dns:
    resolver: system           # system | [ "1.1.1.1:53", ... ]
    cache_ttl_cap: 60s         # caps each record's TTL in the cache
    static_hosts: {}           # name: ip, answered before DNS; still passes the address floor
  deny_private_ranges: true
  deny_cidrs: []               # never valid destinations
  allow_cidrs: []              # exceptions to the private-range floor only
  deny_lists: [blocked]        # names from address_lists
  connect_timeout: 10s         # TCP connect, over all of a name's addresses together; then the TLS handshake, within another
  max_h2_connections_per_origin: 4   # at least 1

tls:
  upstream:
    verify: strict             # strict | strict+extra_roots
    extra_roots: []            # PEM files
    min_version: "1.2"         # "1.2" | "1.3" deny_cidrs and allow_cidrs entries are normalised like address-list
entries: an IPv4-mapped entry (::ffff:203.0.113.0/120) becomes the IPv4
CIDR (203.0.113.0/24) and matches the address however a client spells
it. An entry must be a network: roxy check refuses one with host bits
set (10.1.2.3/8) and names the network it would have meant.
static_hosts keys are host names as a request carries them (ASCII
labels, IDNA already converted to A-labels), not IP addresses.
133.title: Upstream

134.text:
roxy resolves names itself with hickory-resolver (the workload's own DNS
is irrelevant; block it at the network layer). The resolver and its cache
are built once, at start: upstream.dns is a
restart-only setting, and a
reload keeps the cached answers. A and AAAA are both looked up. Several addresses are dialled one at a time, IPv4 and IPv6 alternating
from the resolver's first, within one connect_timeout for all; each
attempt gets an equal share of the time left.
134.title: DNS

135.text:
rustls with the bundled Mozilla roots (webpki-roots), plus extra_roots
under strict+extra_roots. Verification is always on. The SNI is the
canonical host. ALPN offers h2 and http/1.1 (only http/1.1 for
WebSocket upgrades). The handshake has its own connect_timeout after the
TCP connect's: an upstream that accepts the connection but never completes
TLS fails with 504, reason timeout, message upstream TLS handshake.
135.title: Upstream TLS

136.text:
Connections to an origin are pooled by scheme and authority and closed
after 90 s idle. HTTP/1.1 opens one connection per concurrent request.
HTTP/2 multiplexes: an origin that negotiates h2 gets up to
max_h2_connections_per_origin connections, each driven by its own task.
A request goes to the connection with the fewest exchanges in flight (a
response body still streaming counts), so a lightly used origin stays on
one connection and concurrent load spreads evenly across the limit. Each
connection offers a 2 MiB stream window, an 8 MiB connection window and
1 MiB frames. An origin that closes an HTTP/2 connection with GOAWAY (nginx does at
keepalive_requests) fails every stream above the last one it names, which
it never processed. roxy sends such a request again on another connection,
up to twice, if it has no body; a request with a body is answered 502
(upstream_error, reason protocol_error), as its body has already
streamed to the connection.
136.title: Connections

137.text:
failureresponseflow logaddress floor403, _address_policyupstream_denied, reason private_range:<class>, deny_cidrs or list:<name>DNS, connect, TLS502upstream_error, reason dns_failed, connect_failed or tls_faileda target roxy cannot dial (no host, an unknown scheme)502upstream_error, reason invalid_targettimeout (connect, TLS handshake or response headers)504upstream_error, reason timeout; message names the stagea response roxy cannot canonicalise502upstream_error, reason protocol_error Every row answers with the same body
(deny responses); the reason is in the
flow log only.
137.title: Errors

138.text:
A kind: service layer is an external service at its position in the stack
exactly as a WASM layer is (addon model). The
exchange's two lanes stream through it: the request streams into it and it
streams back the request to forward, if it forwards one; the response from
upstream streams into it and it streams back the response the client gets.
It may pass bytes through, rewrite or hold them, or originate its own, on
either lane, at any time. Each lane each way is shaped like an HTTP/2
stream: a head, body bytes, trailers, and an end, or a cut; its reader may
stop it. addons:
  - name: sentinel
    kind: service
    endpoint: sidecar                   # one of this addon's endpoints
    mode: enforce                       # enforce | observe
    endpoints:
      sidecar: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:9000/layer", private_ok: true }
    limits:
      first_byte_timeout: 2s            # to get a stream, then to the service's answer, with no clock while its forward is upstream; an observer's end (default 30s)
      max_connections: 4                # per endpoint (default 4)
      max_streams: 100                  # exchanges at once per connection (default 100) path and the WASM limits are refused on a service layer;
max_connections and max_streams are refused on a WASM layer, and at
zero. capabilities and config mean the same for both kinds
(host services).
138.title: Service layer protocol

139.text:
Long-lived WebSocket connections to each endpoint, each carrying many
exchanges as streams. Subprotocol roxy.layer.v6; a service that does not accept it fails the
handshake.The URL is the endpoint's (http → ws, https → wss, with the
upstream's certificate verification), dialled through the connector (the
address floor and deny lists apply), never through other layers or the
rules. The handshake carries the endpoint's headers. Each connection is
an endpoint_call event against the flow whose exchange opened it.Pooling. A new exchange takes a stream on an idle connection if
there is one; otherwise it opens a connection while the endpoint has
fewer than max_connections; otherwise it takes the connection with the
fewest streams, and once every connection has max_streams streams it
waits for a free one within first_byte_timeout. Concurrent exchanges
spread across connections because each connection is one reader and
one writer on each side: a service that handles each connection on one
task gets one core per connection. Idle connections stay open. A
connection that closes or fails fails its in-flight exchanges closed;
later exchanges go to another connection.Reload. New exchanges get new connections, dialled under the new
policy and secrets. Old connections take no new streams: an idle one
closes at once, a busy one when its last exchange ends.
139.title: Transport

140.text:
Text frames are JSON control messages, each with a stream field. Binary
frames are body bytes: a 4-byte big-endian stream id, one direction byte
(0 request body, 1 response body), then the bytes. roxy numbers the
streams on a connection from 1 upward and never reuses a number. A stream opens with an open message from roxy: {"type":"open","stream":7,"flow":"01J…","conn":"01J…","layer":"sentinel",
 "mode":"enforce","subscribe":{"request":"full","response":"head"},
 "client_ip":"10.0.0.5","listener":"proxy",
 "sni":"api.example.com","tags":["a","b"],
 "capabilities":["state","record"],"config":{"reject_at":0.8}} client_ip is client.ip as the rules see it
(fields). sni is left out when there is
none. capabilities are the layer's grants, and config its config:
value, what a WASM layer reads through flow.config. subscribe is the
layer's
subscription: for a
direction it names head, roxy sends the head and its end with no bytes
between, and the service answers the same way; bytes the service sends for
that body fail the exchange closed (unsubscribed:<direction>), and the
body the service did not see goes on with the head it passed on. Declared
lengths validate bodies; open lanes use unknown wire length so a later cut
remains visible (what a layer
sees). The pair (flow, layer) is unique
and stable (two layers using the same endpoint in one flow get separate
streams with different layers), so a service can key its state on it. Every message carries stream; it is left out below. roxy → service   {"type":"open",…}
                 {"type":"request","method":…,"url":…,"headers":[[n,v],…]}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}
service → roxy   {"type":"request",…}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}       forward this request (`next`), at most once
                 {"type":"request_end"} alone                             nothing forwarded
roxy → service   {"type":"response","status":…,"headers":[…]}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}
                                                                          the response from upstream to what it forwarded
                 {"type":"response_end"} alone, with or without "error"    nothing came back: it forwarded nothing, or its forward was cut
service → roxy   {"type":"response",…}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}   the client's response, exactly once
either way       {"type":"trailers","dir":"request"|"response","headers":[…]}  a body's trailers, after its bytes
                 an end may carry "error":"…": a cut, the body stopped short of it
                 {"type":"stop","dir":"request"|"response"}               the sender reads no more of that body
                 {"type":"credit","dir":"request"|"response","bytes":n}  flow control (below)
                 {"type":"reset","message":"…"}                           abandon the stream
service → roxy   host-service calls, any time the stream is open (below)
roxy → service   {"type":"result","id":n,"value":…} or {"type":"result","id":n,"error":"…"} Each direction of the stream is a lane each way. A lane's events, in
order: at most one head, bytes, at most one trailers, then one end. An
end may come before a head: the lane then carries nothing. A lane whose
end carries "error" is cut: what came before it is not the whole. Trailers
are delivered to the consumer only after a clean end and successful length
validation, because sending HTTP trailers completes the message. Declared
lengths validate bytes; an unfinished lane uses unknown-length framing on
HTTP/1.1 even when the service supplied content-length. Its terminal chunk
is withheld until the clean end. HEAD and bodiless statuses complete on the
HTTP head itself; their internal response lanes are still consumed under
response_body_idle_timeout, and a later failure cancels remaining work
without changing the already-complete HTTP response. ruledetailheadsurl is absolute; headers are end-to-end fields as a WASM layer sees them (no hop-by-hop or framing fields), at most limits.max_headers of them in a head the service sends: more is a protocol violation. content-length is present when the length is known and not zero; one the service sends is enforced: more or fewer bytes than declared is a protocol violationheader valuesbyte strings: each byte is the code point of the same value (ISO-8859-1), so obs-text bytes (http.allow_obs_text) read as Latin-1 and go back as the same bytes. A code point above U+00FF is a protocol violationorderon each lane, from each side: head, bytes, trailers, end. Bytes or trailers before their head or after their end, a second head, a second trailers, a second end: each is a protocol violation. The two lanes are independent, and so are the two sides: roxy sends its response head as soon as the layer upstream answers, even while the client's body is still arriving; the service sends its request at most once and its response exactly once, in either order, and may send either while the other lane is still streaming. A request_end with no request before it forwards nothing. Answering says nothing about forwarding, and a service that wants nothing forwarded forwards nothingcutsan end that carries "error" cuts its lane: the bytes before it are not the whole. From roxy, the body stopped short on its way (an in-flight deny cut it, the upstream's body failed, the client gave up, the service's own forward was cut); the text is for diagnostics only, is not stable, and may be another layer's own. The stream, and the service's own lanes, go on. A response_end with "error" and no response before it says nothing came back for the forward: it was cut. From the service, a cut is its own doing and not a fault: the exchange's record says forward_aborted or answer_aborted, and what is downstream of the cut lane sees it cut. If the service cuts its response lane without ever providing a head, roxy also records no_response and generates a refusal. An error on the end of a head-only lane, which carries no body to cut, is a protocol violationstopstop says its sender reads no more of that body: the receiver sends no more of it, need not end it, and credits nothing for it. roxy sends stop for the request lane when the upstream stops reading the forward. A service that stops the response lane gives the forward up: nothing upstream carries a response nobody waits for, so the upstream request is cancelled. A service that stops the request lane keeps everything elseenda stream ends when all four lanes are terminal (ended, cut or stopped), output body validation has finished, and every accepted host-service call has queued its result. Ending the service's two output lanes leaves the input lanes available: an early answer can finish before the upstream response arrives. A stopped forward upload does not stop that response. The service must read or stop each input; stop on the response input gives up the forward. A service that forwards and never answers is failed by its clock once the upstream outcome arrives. Either side may abandon a stream with reset; roxy sends no further lane data after a reset, and a service reset fails an enforce exchange closed. An opening abandoned before open went out sends no reset. Valid host calls crossing a retired stream's end receive a result error; other messages are ignored and body bytes are not creditedflow controlper stream and per body, each way. Each body of a stream starts with 256 KiB of credit each way; the receiver grants more with credit as it consumes, and the sender may have no more bytes of that body outstanding than granted. roxy grants in steps of 64 KiB as its feeder enqueues frames into the bounded lane channel. That channel holds two frames in addition to the credit window: 256 KiB frames can leave 768 KiB of unread payload per body before the final consumer reads. See buffer bounds. Sending past credit is a protocol violation. Control messages are not counted A stalled physical WebSocket writer backpressures every stream on that
connection. Directional credits allow independent progress while the socket
is writable; the priority control queue can bypass queued data but cannot
bypass bytes already waiting on the socket.
140.title: Frames

141.text:
A service reaches the host services a WASM
layer has by message, each behind the same capability granted in the
layer's capabilities, and answered by the same host: a call means the
same, is refused for the same reasons and fails the layer with the same
layer_error.kind (and the exchange with it, in enforce mode), whichever
kind of layer makes it. Every call carries
an id of the service's choosing (an unsigned 64-bit integer) and is
answered with a result carrying the same id: value is what the call
returns (null for a call that returns nothing), error a refusal of what
the service passed or a call arriving after stream retirement. service → roxycapabilityroxy → service{"type":"log","id":n,"level":"info","message":"…"} (trace, debug, info, warn, error)log{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}{"type":"record","id":n,"kind":"…","data":<json>}record{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}{"type":"add_tag","id":n,"tag":"…"}none; enforce only{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}{"type":"state_get","id":n,"key":"…"}state{"type":"result","id":n,"value":"…"} (null for a miss){"type":"state_put","id":n,"key":"…","value":"…","ttl_ms":n?}state; enforce only{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}, or "error" for a key or value over its cap{"type":"metric_get","id":n,"metric":"…"}metrics{"type":"result","id":n,"value":n} (null for a key with no entry){"type":"quarantine","id":n}quarantine; enforce only{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}; the exchange, and every one after it, is refused _quarantined A call may be sent at any point while the stream is open, including
part-way through a body. Calls run in order, one at a time per stream,
beside the bodies: they neither wait for nor hold up the heads and bytes,
and roxy promises no order between a call and the heads or bytes the
service sends after it. The service orders it: it awaits the result
before sending whatever the effect must precede, be that the request, the
response or the rest of a body
(ordering across layers). A call's tag or state write is seen by
this exchange's admission rules only if it lands before the request is
forwarded; otherwise by the next rule that reads it: for a tag, which
lives on this exchange, an in-flight re-check of it; for state, which
persists, that or a later exchange's admission. A write does not itself
trigger a re-check (#509).
At most 64 calls may be waiting, and more is a protocol violation. Accepted
calls keep the stream open until their results have been queued, including
when all four lanes have finished. To issue a new call, send it before the
last lane becomes terminal. Calls queued before a reset still run, retain
the stream's reservation while they run, and are logged if they fail; their
results have nowhere to go. A valid call arriving after retirement receives
a result error and has no effect. This covers a call crossing roxy's last
input end on the wire. At most 64 such refusals may wait to be written on a
connection; exceeding that limit closes the connection. A call without its capability, a log message or a record kind and
document together over 64 KiB, an add_tag, state_put or quarantine
from an observer, or a full state store fails the layer (layer_error,
kind capability:<name>, budget:message, budget:tags or host) and
resets the stream: in enforce mode that fails the exchange, in observe
mode the exchange goes on. The result error reports a refusal of what
the service passed, or a call arriving after stream retirement.
roxy's own record of a call names its id as call: on the
layer_record a record writes, on the layer_error a failed call
causes, on the operational log line a log writes, and on the cause of
the quarantined event a quarantine trips. endpoints.call
has no message: a service calls what it needs itself.
141.title: Host services

142.text:
roxy.layer.v6 is incompatible with roxy.layer.v5 and the experimental
roxy.layer.v0. Update the WebSocket subprotocol on both peers together.
Each side must handle stop, trailers, explicit ends in both directions,
and headless completion. Keep receiving upstream input after both service
outputs end, and explicitly stop inputs the handler will not consume.
Outstanding host calls now receive results before normal stream retirement.
The bundled Python helper implements this contract. Incompatible protocol
changes use a new subprotocol name so older peers fail at negotiation. WASM layers use roxy:addon@0.3.0; rebuild components with the matching SDK
and WIT. Components using roxy:addon@0.2.1 or the experimental unversioned
package must be rebuilt. Package versions remain part of the interface
identity for future incompatible changes.
142.title: Migration from v5

143.text:
The forwarded request gets the same checks as a WASM layer's next:
re-validated as strictly as a client request, then judged by the rules.
What comes back on the response lane is whatever the upstream stages
produced: the upstream's response, the rules' refusal, or an HTTP error
response for a failure upstream. The service may pass on or reshape any
of these responses. The service's own response is handled as a WASM layer's.Deadlines. first_byte_timeout bounds getting a stream, then the
service's answer, as it does a WASM layer's: from roxy's request head
until the service answers or forwards. The clock is suspended while its
forward awaits an upstream outcome. A response head or a headless
response_end restores the whole budget, unless the service has already
answered; receiving a head does not wait for the response body to end.
An expiry of the original request budget cannot consume or suspend this
renewed answer budget.
An observer gets that budget from roxy's last message to end its stream. A
stream has no overall deadline. Head-only output lanes still require
their explicit end: bypassed bytes can flow before it, but completion
waits for both the end message and the bypassed body. This includes a
HEAD or bodiless response already completed on the client connection.
Body-idle and upstream timeouts still
apply while the service's answer clock is suspended. The client edge
applies response_body_idle_timeout even to a HEAD or bodiless response
it must discard, and observes client loss through final reclamation.An early response goes to the client at once, however far the
forward upstream has got, and its body is the client's response from then
on; the response from upstream still arrives on the service's lane for it
to read. If the stack upstream fails after that, what arrives is the
HTTP error response for that failure, or the lane ending with the error if its
body had started; the service's answer stands either way. The forward
runs on only while the service waits for its response (the end rule
above).Failure is closed in enforce mode: a failed connection or handshake,
a protocol violation (bad JSON, a message out of order, bytes of a body
that is not open, an invalid head, a broken length, bytes past the
credit), a missed deadline, a reset from the service or a lost connection
denies the exchange (503, layer:<name>) before the response head and
cuts a streaming body after it. A cut body never reaches either peer as
complete; HEAD and bodiless responses have already completed at the head. layer_error.kind is service:connect,
service:protocol, service:timeout or service:closed; bytes of a
head-only body are unsubscribed:<direction>. A response_end with no
response before it is no answer: no_response.A body that fails on its way to the service is not its failure: its
lane ends with the error, no layer_error is logged, and the stream
goes on (who is blamed).One stream's failure is its own: a violation resets that stream
only. Broken framing fails the whole connection: a text frame that is not
a JSON object with a valid stream, a binary frame shorter than its
5-byte prefix or with an unknown direction byte, or a stream id roxy
never opened. Every exchange on it fails closed (service:protocol) and
roxy closes it.Observe mode uses the same streams: the
service gets copies of both directions; credit is honoured, reset
ends the stream and is logged (layer_error, service:closed),
host-service calls run as in enforce mode (less the ones an observer may
not make), and the heads, bytes and ends the service sends go nowhere.
The stream ends after all four lanes and accepted host calls finish, as
in enforce mode. A stop from the service ends the corresponding copy.
So a service can read the copies through and then record what it saw
before ending the stream, as a WASM observer can. From roxy's last
message the service has first_byte_timeout to end the stream, or roxy
fails it (service:timeout); a cut copy (observer_lagged) is reset.
Waiting for credit is falling behind, so grant extra credit as an observe
stream opens (roxy_layer.py grants 16 MiB per body). Body bytes the
service sends on an observe stream are discarded and credited back in
steps of 64 KiB; past credit is still a violation.WebSockets run through the stream
(addon configuration). The
101 from upstream arrives as roxy's response head, and the service
answers with a 101 of its own. At the client edge, only final statuses
200–599 or a 101 for a real upstream upgrade are accepted; intermediate
lane heads may be rewritten by a downstream layer before reaching it.
After the upgrade, the request body carries the client's bytes and the
response body the upstream's, with no length cap on either, until each side closes; the stream holds its place on the
connection for as long as the WebSocket is open. roxy sends no
request_end before the 101, so a service that waits for the end of
the request body never forwards an upgrade and fails on
first_byte_timeout: forward as the request arrives. When the relay
ends, roxy closes the client's connection and resets the stream if its
bodies have not both ended. The quickstart's sidecar,
roxy_layer.py,
is the service side of the protocol for asyncio: it handles streams, credit
and resets and hands a handler one exchange at a time. The helper rejects a host call with ProtocolError if the stream ends while
the call waits to send. Such an unsent call does not keep the stream open.
A call already sent keeps its result waiter; if it crosses retirement on
the wire, roxy's refusal raises HostError. The Python helper exposes received trailers through trailers and
response_trailers. Its byte-iterator forwarding helpers do not send
trailers; a service using those helpers must not assume trailer-preserving
passthrough. The Python helper's Exchange.forward raises ForwardEnded when the upstream
response lane ends without a head. A handler may catch it and answer locally.
If it propagates, the helper ends its response lane headless; it does not reset
the stream. A handler that supplies no answer still gets no_response;
the forward ending is not a service protocol fault.
143.title: Semantics

144.text:
An upgrade is honoured only when the allowing rule says
allow: { upgrade: websocket }. Under a plain allow, roxy drops Upgrade
and Connection: upgrade, forwards the request as plain HTTP and emits
upgrade_stripped; the client gets whatever the upstream answers (typically
200, 400 or 426) and its WebSocket library reports a failed
handshake. Upgrades to anything other than websocket (h2c, say) are
always stripped.
144.title: WebSockets

145.text:
roxy forwards the upgrade request over HTTP/1.1 after the usual header
canonicalisation; Sec-WebSocket-* headers pass through. Connecting, the
upgrade request and taking over the upgraded connection share one
limits.response_header_timeout; the client gets the 101 only once roxy
holds the upstream side, so a failed upgrade is an error response, never a
101 followed by a close: failureresultthe client's upgrade is not a valid handshake (not GET, not HTTP/1.1, a body, Sec-WebSocket-Version other than 13, a Sec-WebSocket-Key missing, repeated or not the base64 of 16 bytes)400, terminal_rule: _websocket, reason ws_bad_handshakeresponse_header_timeout runs out504the upstream answers anything other than 101relayed as it isa 101 with a wrong Sec-WebSocket-Accept, or accepting an extension when none may be negotiated (below)502, upstream_error, reason protocol_error Through an http_proxy listener a ws:// URL means a CONNECT tunnel
with a plaintext upgrade inside it, which roxy refuses unless
http.allow_plain_in_connect is on (the tunnel is closed, parse_error
reason non_http_in_connect; CONNECT). Use
wss://. For WSS, roxy establishes the CONNECT tunnel and terminates TLS
before processing the HTTP/1.1 upgrade. Addon layers receive that upgrade
and carry the WebSocket bytes in both directions; the outer CONNECT is
handled by the listener. On an http listener the upgrade arrives as
plain HTTP and needs nothing. If no rule reads a ws.* field, roxy splices bytes: no frame parsing,
re-masking or reassembly; subprotocols and extensions pass end to end. If
any rule reads ws.*, every message is checked
(message rules). Either way: Relayed bytes count towards request_bytes and response_bytes metrics
as they flow; a byte-budget deny closes a WebSocket mid-stream (the byte
splice at the transport, message rules with a 1008 close frame first).Each chunk waits for the flow log (audit backpressure);
capture records both directions as relayed.Addon layers sit between the
client and the relay, so message rules and capture see what the layers
pass on, not what a layer changes on the way to the client.A relayed WebSocket with no traffic either way for limits.idle_timeout
(1 h) is closed with a 1001 close frame to both sides (close_reason
idle timeout).The flow log gets one ws_open (naming the host) and one ws_close
with bytes_c2s and bytes_s2c, plus close_code and close_reason
when roxy ended it with a close frame. The exchange's request event
follows, with res.status: 101 and the relayed byte totals as its
body_bytes. WebSockets over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441 extended CONNECT) are not supported;
clients must use a separate HTTP/1.1 connection for WebSockets. This
restriction concerns the HTTP version, not TLS: wss:// over HTTP/1.1 is
supported, including through addon layers.
145.title: Relay

146.text:
A compressed message (permessage-deflate) cannot be read without the
compression state of every message before it, so when something reads the
messages roxy removes Sec-WebSocket-Extensions from the upgrade request
and refuses with 502 a 101 that accepts an extension anyway. That is
when a rule reads ws.*, or an addon layer runs on the upgrade request
(its when matched) with http.decode_for_addons on (the default;
addons). Otherwise the
client's offer and the upstream's answer pass through untouched.
146.title: Extensions

147.text:
Rules that read ws.* are in-flight rules
(evaluation), checked on every message after
the 101: rules:
  - id: chat
    when: host == "chat.example.com"
    then: { allow: { upgrade: websocket } }
  - id: no-keys-out
    when: ws.direction == "c2s" and ws.opcode == 1 and ws.text matches ".*sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}.*"
    then: deny fieldvaluews.directionc2s (client to upstream) or s2cws.opcode1 text, 2 binary, 8 close, 9 ping, 10 pongws.sizepayload length in bytesws.texta text message's text; null for every other opcode ==, !=, in and not in treat null as an ordinary value; any other
operator on it fails closed
(missing values), so guard
text rules with ws.opcode == 1 and ... or the first ping closes the
WebSocket. Control messages (close, ping, pong) are checked like data
messages: ws.opcode == 2 denies binary messages, while ws.opcode != 1
also denies every ping. A matching deny closes both sides with 1008. A rule cannot drop or edit a
single message (that is for addons). An in-flight rule's log, tag and
set_state effects apply once per WebSocket, the first time it matches.
147.title: Message rules

148.text:
With message rules, roxy: negotiates no extension (above);decodes each direction strictly (RFC 6455 §5): RSV bits zero, known
opcodes, client frames masked and server frames not, shortest length
encoding, control frames unfragmented and at most 125 bytes, a close
frame with a valid code and a UTF-8 reason and nothing after it;reassembles a fragmented message before checking it, up to
limits.max_ws_message_bytes (16 MiB); a control frame inside a
fragmented message is checked and relayed on its own;checks that a text message is UTF-8;re-encodes each relayed message as one unfragmented frame, masked toward
the upstream with its own random key. A protocol error closes both sides with its code: 1002 framing, 1007
invalid UTF-8, 1009 over the limit. A message is relayed only once
complete.
148.title: Parsing

149.text:
A denied message is logged as ws_message with its direction, opcode,
size, decision and the rules that matched.
log.flow.ws_message_every: N also logs every Nth checked message of each
WebSocket (0, the default: denied only). Payloads are never logged.
149.title: Logging

150.text:
On a proxy port roxy terminates every TLS tunnel with a leaf certificate
minted by its CA. roxy generates that CA, or uses one you provide, and
clients must trust it. The certificates roxy mints and the handshake it
offers are in TLS. ca_server:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:3130           # plain HTTP: /roxy-ca.pem, /healthz and /readyz; absent = off

tls:
  ca_dir: /var/lib/roxy/ca     # roxy-ca.pem + roxy-ca.key, generated if absent
  # ca_cert: /etc/roxy/ca/tls.crt  # a provided CA instead; set both or neither
  # ca_key: /etc/roxy/ca/tls.key
  require_sni_match: true
  leaf_cache_size: 10000       # at least 1
150.title: Managing the CA

151.text:
On first roxy run (or roxy ca init) roxy generates an ECDSA P-256 CA:
10-year validity, CA:TRUE, pathlen:0, key usage keyCertSign, cRLSign.
It is written to tls.ca_dir as roxy-ca.pem (mode 0644) and
roxy-ca.key (mode 0600). An existing pair is reused. A corrupt pair is a fatal startup
error, never silently regenerated, since a new CA breaks the trust every
client already has; roxy ca init --force replaces it deliberately. To use an existing CA in ca_dir, put its certificate and key there as
roxy-ca.pem and roxy-ca.key. The startup checks below apply.
151.title: Generated CA

152.text:
Set tls.ca_cert and tls.ca_key to use a CA you already have, such as a
sub-CA issued by your organisation's root or a Kubernetes tls secret
mounted read-only. Setting only one is a config error. ca_dir is then not
used. ca_cert is PEM. The first certificate is the CA that signs leaves.
Any further certificates are its intermediates, in order up to but not
including the root. roxy sends them after the CA in every handshake, so
clients that trust only the root can build the chain.ca_key is the CA's private key as unencrypted PKCS#8 PEM
(BEGIN PRIVATE KEY). ECDSA P-256 is the key type roxy generates and
tests; P-384, Ed25519 and RSA keys load but are untested.
Convert a SEC1 or PKCS#1 key with
openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt -in ca.key -out ca-pkcs8.key. A provided CA is never generated or replaced. A missing or unusable file
is a fatal startup error, and roxy ca init refuses to run.
152.title: Provided CA

153.text:
Every CA, provided or generated, is checked at startup, and by roxy
check, which loads it the same way. It must be a CA certificate
(CA:TRUE), allow keyCertSign if it has a key usage extension, be within
its validity period, and match its key. Each intermediate must be a CA
within its validity period whose key signed the certificate before it. Any
failure stops roxy. Two conditions are warnings, not errors; startup logs them and check
