prints them as warning: lines: The key file is readable by its group or by others. Make it mode 0600.The CA expires within seven days. Leaves normally last seven days; one
minted now ends when the CA does, and once the CA has expired roxy
mints nothing and every TLS handshake fails (leaf_mint_failed).
Replace the CA before then; a restart after expiry refuses to start.
153.title: Startup checks

154.text:
The CA certificate, never the key, is available three ways. For a
provided CA this is the signing CA alone, without intermediates; clients
that already trust your organisation's root need nothing from roxy. roxy ca export --config roxy.yaml > roxy-ca.pem                   # at image build time (--der for DER)
curl -s http://<ca_server.bind>/roxy-ca.pem > roxy-ca.pem         # from the CA server
curl -s -x http://<proxy> http://roxy.internal/roxy-ca.pem        # through the proxy itself The ca_server listener is separate from the proxy port so it can be
firewalled differently. It also serves the /healthz and /readyz probes
(health).
154.title: CA distribution

155.text:
An http listener lets roxy stand in for an origin. Clients send ordinary
requests to a name that resolves to roxy, and per-host rules decide where
each one goes and what to add. The example here is an LLM gateway: clients
hold placeholder keys, roxy holds the real ones and injects them on the way
out, and an addon says who is calling.
155.title: HTTP gateway

156.text:
*.gw.example.com points at a load balancer, which terminates TLS and
forwards plain HTTP to roxy. roxy sees each request with scheme http and
the Host the client sent. One rule per subdomain redirects the request
to its provider over https and set_headers the real key in place of
whatever the client sent; anything no rule matches is denied. version: 1

listeners:
  - name: gateway
    mode: http
    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
    forwarded_for: { trusted_hops: 1 }   # one load balancer in front

secrets:
  anthropic: { env: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
  openai:    { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }

rules:
  - id: anthropic
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "anthropic.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/v1/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: api.anthropic.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - set_header: { x-api-key: "${secret:anthropic}" }
      - allow

  - id: openai
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "openai.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/v1/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: api.openai.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
      - allow

  - id: bedrock
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "bedrock.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/model/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
      - allow rewrite_host: true sends the provider's name in Host, which the
provider expects and which lets the upstream connection use HTTP/2
(redirect). Bedrock wants a
signature rather than a key: sign covers the request as forwarded, after
the redirect, so the signature is over the host AWS sees
(signing AWS requests). From here an exchange is the same as on a proxy port: rate limits, body
rules, addons, the address floor and the flow log all apply
(how roxy works).
156.title: The pattern

157.text:
The listener adds no authentication: a client is whoever reaches it, and
the rules see that as listener.name and client.ip. Authenticate at the
load balancer, or with an addon on the listener that checks a credential,
tags the flow user:<name> and strips the header, as the quickstart's auth
gate does (what just happened). The API
key still comes from roxy's secrets, injected by the rule, and the layers
below see the tag, so a per-user quota is another addon.
157.title: Authenticating clients

158.text:
This is not containment. The listener serves whoever reaches it, and
the clients may have other routes out
(threat model).Say how many proxies are in front. forwarded_for.trusted_hops is
the number of proxies between the clients and roxy, each appending to
X-Forwarded-For; with it, client.ip in rules, rate limits and the
flow log is the client the load balancer saw, and a request the header
does not account for is refused
(HTTP). Without it,
client.ip is the load balancer's address and every client shares one.
Only the load balancer may reach the listener; a client that can connect
directly chooses its own client.ip.
limits.max_connections_per_client counts the connection's peer either
way, so it caps the whole gateway: leave it unset (it follows
max_connections) or raise it with the fleet
(limits).TLS stays in front. roxy does not terminate TLS on an http
listener; a client that starts a handshake is closed
(tls_on_http_listener). Keep the hop from the load balancer to roxy on a
network you trust, since it carries the clients' requests in the clear.
Clients trust the load balancer's certificate; roxy's CA plays no part.In-cluster upstreams are private addresses. The address floor denies
RFC 1918 and the other private ranges by default, so a rule that forwards
to a service on the cluster network needs private_ok: true on its
allow: then: { allow: { private_ok: true } }
(address floor).Health checks come from ca_server as usual
(health).Leave quarantine_on off. A
quarantine shuts the whole process, so
on a gateway one client's malformed requests would refuse every other
client until an operator intervened. The same goes for the quarantine
action in a gateway's rules.
158.title: What to know

159.text:
An untrusted workload runs where its only route out is roxy. It points
HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY at an http_proxy listener and trusts
roxy's CA. roxy decrypts each request, judges it, injects the credentials
the workload needs, and logs every decision. Containment comes from the
network: the proxy variables only tell a well-behaved client where roxy
is (threat model).
159.title: Sandbox containment

160.text:
Take away the workload's route out. Put it in a network namespace,
VM or container network whose only reachable host is roxy. Block
everything else, including direct TCP, UDP and DNS, at the network layer.
roxy resolves DNS itself, so the workload needs none.Give roxy a route out, and the workload a route to roxy's proxy port
(an http_proxy listener, 3128 in the examples). Keep the CA endpoint
(3130) reachable from the workload only if it should fetch the CA
itself.listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy             # the default
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
ca_server:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:3130             # serves /roxy-ca.pem to the workloadPoint the workload at roxy and make it trust roxy's CA
(CA distribution):export HTTP_PROXY=http://<proxy> HTTPS_PROXY=http://<proxy>
export http_proxy=$HTTP_PROXY https_proxy=$HTTPS_PROXY   # curl reads only the lower-case http_proxy
export SSL_CERT_FILE=/path/roxy-ca.pem         # OpenSSL-based tools, Python ssl, Go
export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/roxy-ca.pem    # Python requests
export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/roxy-ca.pem   # Node
export CURL_CA_BUNDLE=/path/roxy-ca.pem        # curlAdding the certificate to the system trust store also works. Do not put
external hosts in NO_PROXY.Decide what shuts the proxy for good. A workload that probes roxy
with malformed requests, or reaches for something a rule marks as
beyond the pale, can be quarantined:
every exchange refused until an operator, or the control plane, lets it
out. Set quarantine_on on the listener and use the quarantine action
in the rules that should trip it, and run roxy with --state-dir so the
quarantine survives a restart:listeners:
  - name: proxy
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
    quarantine_on:
      parse_errors: { count: 20, window: 1m }
rules:
  - id: exfil
    when: host == "api.anthropic.com" and body.text contains "BEGIN PRIVATE KEY"
    then: quarantine
160.title: The recipe

161.text:
The workload sits only on an internal: true network, which has no route
out (Docker's embedded DNS still resolves service names on it); roxy alone
is on both it and a network with a route out: services:
  roxy:
    image: ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy:latest
    read_only: true
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    volumes: [./roxy.yaml:/etc/roxy/roxy.yaml:ro, roxy-ca:/var/lib/roxy/ca]
    networks: [sandbox, egress]
  agent:
    image: your-workload
    networks: [sandbox]              # no route out except through roxy
    environment:
      HTTPS_PROXY: http://roxy:3128
      https_proxy: http://roxy:3128
      NO_PROXY: roxy                 # roxy's CA endpoint, reached directly
      no_proxy: roxy
networks:
  sandbox:
    internal: true                   # no route out: the containment
  egress: {}
volumes:
  roxy-ca: {} The workload fetches the CA from http://roxy:3130/roxy-ca.pem. A client
that ignores the proxy variables, or a library that opens its own sockets,
gets nowhere: there is no route out, whatever a name resolves to. Other services on the Compose network resolve to private addresses, which
the address floor denies by default. A rule that lets the workload reach
one needs private_ok: true on its allow, for example
then: { allow: { private_ok: true } }
(address floor); rules for
public upstreams need nothing.
161.title: With Docker Compose

162.text:
An http_proxy listener is the narrowest interface roxy can offer a
workload: HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 and nothing else, with CONNECT opening only a
tunnel roxy intercepts (raw TCP never passes), and every destination a name
roxy parses itself, judges in the rules, resolves and checks the IP of
(HTTP). An http listener is for traffic sent to roxy
on purpose (HTTP gateway), not for containing a
workload.
162.title: Why a proxy port

163.text:
In node mode roxy has no config file: it enrols with a control plane,
leases its policy and secrets from it, and ships its flow log back. The
control plane is any server that implements the
node protocol. roxy run --control-plane https://cp.example:8443 \
         --enrol-token-file /run/secrets/roxy-enrol-token \
         --state-dir /var/lib/roxy/node \
         --control-plane-ca /etc/roxy/cp-ca.pem --control-plane and --config are mutually exclusive.
163.title: Node mode

164.title: Flags

165.text:
filecontentsnode.tokenThe node token with its node_id and not_after, as one JSON object, mode 0600. Replaced on each renewal.flow.seqThe flow seq counter, reserved ahead in blocks of 1024 by a background task, never on the request path. A restart continues after the last reservation. If it cannot be written at startup, the node does not start. If a later write fails, roxy logs it, keeps shipping and retries; once events outrun the last reservation it reports seq_unreserved: true on each lease poll until a reservation catches up, and a restart before then may reuse seq values.ca/The interception CA, as tls.ca_dir holds it in file mode.quarantinePresent while the node is quarantined: the incident as JSON, mode 0600. Written when the quarantine trips and removed when the control plane releases it; a node that starts with it present starts quarantined. A --state-dir given to roxy run --config holds this file alone. Nothing else is written: the rendered config and the secret values stay in
memory, so a copy of the state dir is a revocable node identity, plus
whether the node was quarantined, and nothing else.
165.title: The state dir

166.text:
The state dir is authoritative for the interception CA: tls.ca_dir is
always <state-dir>/ca, and tls.ca_cert/tls.ca_key in the rendered
config are ignored with a warning. No CA anywhere on first start: one is generated into <state-dir>/ca,
as tls.ca_dir does in file mode.--interception-ca-cert and --interception-ca-key on a start where the
state dir holds no CA: the pair is imported (key 0600) and used. A later
start without the flags uses the stored pair; it is never regenerated.The flags name a pair different from the stored one: roxy refuses to
start and prints both fingerprints, since workloads already trust the
stored CA. To replace it, delete roxy-ca.pem and roxy-ca.key from
<state-dir>/ca, or pass --replace-interception-ca.A stored pair that does not parse is fatal, as in file mode. Workloads fetch the CA from ca_server as usual
(CA distribution).
166.title: The interception CA

167.text:
The listeners open at once, on --bootstrap-bind and
--bootstrap-ca-server, with an empty policy: every request is denied
with terminal_rule: _default, /healthz answers 200 and /readyz
answers 503 no_policy.With no node.token in the state dir the node reads the enrolment
token and enrols; the node token goes to the state dir. A 401 (or
another 4xx) is retried with backoff for two minutes, then the node
exits non-zero, so an orchestrator sees a crash loop rather than a node
that denies everything for ever; a 410 or 426 exits at once. An
unreachable control plane is retried for as long as the outage lasts.
With a node.token present the enrolment token file is not read; if the
stored token has expired the node exits non-zero too, naming the remedy:
a new enrolment token and an empty state dir.The node fetches its lease and applies it. The first lease's
listeners, ca_server, tls, connection limits and log destinations
replace the bootstrap ones. Later leases that change one of those
settings keep the running value and warn, as a file reload does
(restart-only settings); a
restart picks them up. A node.token record that does not parse stops startup. A 200 enrolment,
renewal, lease or flow-upload response that does not parse is retried with
backoff. These diagnostics report only the kind of fault and its JSON line
and column, never the input, which may hold a token or a lease secret.
167.title: Startup

168.text:
Every poll answers with the whole lease, applied in full or not at all.
The rendered config goes through the same validation as roxy check; a
config it would reject, or a declared secret with no value, is logged
(lease could not be applied) and the running policy stays. The node then
reports the old lease_id on its next fetch, which is how the control
plane learns the lease did not take. The fields are in the lease body.
valid_for_seconds becomes the policy's valid_until, on the node's own
clock from just before the fetch was sent (lease);
the node polls again after refresh_after_seconds, never later than halfway
through. A changed config swaps the policy atomically as a reload does,
changed secrets alone swap the secret map, and a changed state_epoch
clears every rule set_state entry and metric window first. secrets
supplies the config's secrets: entries that declare lease: true; env
and file sources are resolved on the node as in file mode, and a name
with no value from either refuses the lease. A quarantined node keeps polling and keeps
applying leases, so its policy is current the moment the quarantine lifts;
it reports the incident in quarantine on every poll, and lifts it when the
lease's quarantine.release names that incident's id
(lease body). Nothing on the node
lifts it otherwise: not a reload, not a restart with the marker still in
the state dir. What the node does with each response code is in the
errors table. A 410 (revoked) expires
the lease at once (the policy stays loaded with its valid_until in the
past, so every request is denied, and the secrets are cleared), stops
polling and offers what is spooled to the control plane; a restart with the same state dir ends the
same way. A 401, 400, 426 or unreachable control plane lets the lease
run down: the node denies everything from valid_until until the next
200, which recovers it without a restart. It never re-enrols unasked; to
re-enrol, empty the state dir and start with a new enrolment token. A node
whose token expires exits non-zero, since only re-enrolment can recover it. The node renews its token at the renew_after_seconds the control plane
stated, and no later than two thirds of the way to its not_after
(renew). A renewal answered 401 is
retried with backoff, as an outage is: the replica answering may not yet
know the token the last renewal issued. One the control plane refuses
otherwise (426, or any 4xx other than 401 and 410) is logged once
and not retried; the current token serves until it expires.
168.title: The lease

169.text:
Every flow-log event goes to the local log.flow destination as usual, and
into an in-memory spool tagged with a per-node seq that the lease's flow
settings say how to ship (flow upload).
A batch is posted when batch_max_bytes of events are waiting or
flush_interval_seconds have passed since the oldest unsent one, whichever
comes first, so the request rate to the control plane is bounded by the
interval however busy the proxy is.
At spool_high_water_bytes of unacknowledged events, on_high_water: hold
holds traffic through roxy's flow-log backpressure until the control plane
acknowledges enough; spool drops the oldest and logs once per episode. A
batch stays spooled until acknowledged, so a 400 or a 507 (quota
exhausted) leaves unshipped audit in the spool and on_high_water applies
to what accumulates. Shutdown lets in-flight exchanges finish, then ships
what is spooled, for up to ten seconds. Before the first lease the spool runs in spool mode with a 1 MiB batch
and an 8 MiB high water, so a control plane that is slow to answer cannot
hold traffic.
169.title: Flow shipping

170.text:
SIGHUP reopens the local log destinations; there is no file to reload.
SIGTERM or ctrl-c shuts down as in file mode. /healthz and /readyz on
the lease's ca_server behave as in operations:
ready means an unexpired lease is in force.
170.title: Signals and health

171.text:
roxy's own logs go to stderr (--log-format json|pretty, --log-level or
RUST_LOG); the flow log goes to stdout or log.flow.path
(flow log). SIGHUP reloads the config and reopens
log files. SIGTERM or ctrl-c stops accepting, drains exchanges in flight
for up to 10 seconds, and flushes the flow log and capture before exiting.
171.title: Operations

172.text:
The ca_server listener answers two probes, both plain HTTP GET: path200 whenotherwise/healthzthe process is up and accepting connectionsno answer/readyza policy has been applied, its lease has not run out and the process is not quarantined503 with a one-word reason: quarantined (quarantine), no_policy (nothing applied yet) or policy_expired (lease) Use /readyz for a compose depends_on wait or a Kubernetes readiness
probe, and /healthz for a liveness probe or a container HEALTHCHECK.
Readiness reads the policy the proxy is evaluating against, so a reload
with a later lease makes it ready without a restart. The ca_server listener has its own connection cap, separate from the
proxy's: limits.max_connections in total, with no per-client cap. A
client that fills the proxy's cap does not stop the probes answering, but
one that fills the ca_server cap does, so keep that port reachable only
from the workloads that fetch the CA and from the probe. Refused
ca_server connections are logged in roxy's own log, not the flow log. An empty policy is ready: it is a deny-all that someone applied, so a roxy
told to refuse everything stays in rotation and its refusals are audited.
From a config file a policy is always applied at startup, so no_policy is
only seen by a node waiting for its first lease. roxy health is the probe for images without a shell or curl: it GETs
http://127.0.0.1:3130/healthz (--ready: /readyz; --url names
another address) and exits 0 on a 200, 1 on anything else, with the
reason on stderr.
172.title: Health

173.text:
roxy check --config <file> runs the part of startup that opens no socket
and writes no file: parse, validate, compile the rules and the WASM
addons, load the address lists, load a provided CA (tls.ca_cert,
tls.ca_key), read tls.upstream.extra_roots and build the resolver. It
loads the CA through the same function startup does, so the warnings
startup logs about it (a key readable by others, a certificate close to
expiry) are printed by check as warning: lines. Diagnostics carry the
config path, rule id and position. It leaves to
startup resolving secrets from the environment, generating a CA in
tls.ca_dir, opening log.flow.path and capture_dir, and binding the
listeners. Reload shares that path. roxy watches the config file, the address-list
files and the addon .wasm files, following symlinks, so a file swapped
underneath its path (a Kubernetes ConfigMap mount) counts as changed; a
change, or SIGHUP, triggers a reload. On success the new policy is
swapped in atomically: exchanges in flight finish under the policy they
started with, and the next request on any connection uses the new one. On
failure the old policy stays, a config_reload_failed event carries the
diagnostics, and nothing is partially applied: not the policy, not the
metric store, and not the compiled addons the next reload reuses. A
shutdown signal during a reload abandons it and drains the running policy. Metric series survive a reload when their metric is
unchanged. When the new
config keeps every running metric, the rebuilt store goes in before the
policy swap, so no flow on either side meets a metric its store does not
know. When a metric is removed or reshaped, the store follows the swap, and
only an exchange still finishing under the old policy can find its metric
gone (and is then failed closed).
173.title: Reload

174.text:
Some settings take effect only when roxy starts: listeners, ca_server,
tls.ca_dir, tls.ca_cert, tls.ca_key, tls.leaf_cache_size,
tls.upstream, upstream.dns, limits.max_connections,
limits.max_connections_per_client, limits.max_state_entries,
limits.max_capture_body_bytes, log.flow, log.capture and
capture_dir. A reload keeps their running values, applies everything
else, and warns naming each one that changed. The new config is validated
with the running values; when that fails, the diagnostics name the
restart-only settings the file changed. The resolver is one of them: its cache serves every policy, so a reload
that touches only rules or lists keeps every cached answer. The upstream
connection pools are the snapshot's and start empty on each reload. A connection takes tls.require_sni_match, http.enable_h2,
http.allow_plain_in_connect and the limits and http parsing settings
when it is accepted and keeps them; a reload changes them for new
connections only (limits).
174.title: Restart-only settings

175.text:
A top-level valid_until: <RFC 3339> makes the loaded policy a lease.
Until that instant the policy applies as written. From it, every request
is denied with terminal_rule: _expired and reason policy_expired, and
an open WebSocket relay stops at its next chunk or message. The lease is
checked before the addons run and again before the rules, so a request an
addon holds across the instant is denied when the addon forwards it, as a
request sent after the instant is. Each check is a wall-clock comparison
against the host's clock, using the loaded policy's instant whichever
policy the exchange began under: a reload that moves it later keeps open
relays going, and one that moves it earlier stops them at their next chunk
or message. The first exchange that finds the policy expired logs one
policy_expired event; later ones are ordinary _expired denies. An expired policy is a policy, not a fault. The listeners stay up,
/healthz keeps answering 200 with x-roxy-policy: expired (valid
otherwise, quarantined under a quarantine), roxy health prints ok
(policy expired), and /readyz answers 503 policy_expired. A document already past its valid_until
loads and denies rather than failing to start. roxy check prints valid
until: and warns when the instant has passed. In
node mode the control plane's lease sets it. The way back is a reload: a config whose valid_until is later, or
absent, is swapped in like any other. There is no fallback policy: a policy
that must not expire has no valid_until.
175.title: Lease

176.text:
A quarantine is roxy refusing every exchange, whatever the policy says,
until something outside the process lifts it. It is for a workload that has
shown itself hostile: once tripped, the proxy stays shut across reloads and
restarts, and the client cannot talk its way out. Three things trip it: a rule's quarantine action (actions):
the exchange is refused, by whichever deny wins, and the proxy is
quarantined, even if a rule below it fails closed;an enforce layer's flow.quarantine
(host services): the
exchange it was called on is refused _quarantined, and the proxy is
quarantined;a listener's quarantine_on.parse_errors threshold
(listeners): that many parse_error
events on the listener within the window, counting every reason except
timeouts (header_timeout, body_timeout, tunnel_timeout,
tls_handshake_timeout, h2_handshake_timeout), a client that left
(unexpected_eof, io_error) or that ended the TLS handshake with an
alert of its own (tls_alert_received, as a client that does not trust
roxy's CA does), and roxy's own failures (connect_write_failed,
leaf_mint_failed, invalid_state). Off unless
set; set it on a sandbox's listener, not a gateway's, where one client
would shut the proxy for every other. While quarantined, every request is refused with 403, terminal_rule:
_quarantined and reason quarantined, before the addons and the rules, and
before the lease is checked. An open WebSocket relay stops at its next
chunk or message. Connections open at the trip have one second to finish,
then they are closed, so a stream in flight carries little further; the
exchange that tripped it uses that second to write its own refusal. The
trip is logged once as a quarantined event with the incident id, when it
tripped and why (flow log). /healthz stays
200 with x-roxy-policy: quarantined, roxy health prints ok
(quarantined), and /readyz answers 503 quarantined. CA distribution
keeps working. A config that can quarantine (a quarantine action, quarantine_on on a
listener, or an addon holding the quarantine capability) needs roxy run
--state-dir DIR: roxy refuses to start, or to
reload into such a config, without it. The trip writes DIR/quarantine
(the incident as JSON, mode 0600), and a start that finds the file starts
quarantined, logging the quarantined event again with restored: true.
The in-memory state changes before the file is written. A write failure is
logged as an error and leaves the process quarantined; whether a restart
starts quarantined then depends on whether the file landed before the
failure, so check for DIR/quarantine before restarting. Lifting it is never the proxy's own doing. From a config file: stop roxy,
remove DIR/quarantine, start it again. A reload does not lift it, and a
restart with the file in place does not either. In node
mode the control plane releases it by naming
the incident id in its lease, and the node logs quarantine_released.
176.title: Quarantine

180.text:
roxy check validates a config and prints diagnostics
(check and reload). roxy rule test
shows what the policy does with a request you describe, without sending
any traffic. roxy check --config roxy.yaml        # exits 1 with diagnostics
roxy rule test --config roxy.yaml GET https://api.github.com/repos/a/b
roxy rule test --config roxy.yaml --metric github_writes=30 POST https://api.github.com/repos/a/b/issues roxy rule test evaluates a synthetic request with no network I/O and

allow and 3 on deny. The request arrives on the config's first listener,
which sets listener.name. roxy rule test --help lists every flag.

181.text:
The canonical request, as in roxy run: The URL is parsed and normalised by the proxy's own parser
(https://H.example./a/%2e/b/../c is host == "h.example" and
path == "/a/c").Hop-by-hop fields such as connection are removed, and
header["host"], header["content-length"] and header["upgrade"] come
from the parsed request rather than from --header.A request the proxy would refuse (a non-ASCII host, a path that climbs
above the root, a Host that does not match the URL) exits 1 with the
same reason code.An IP-literal URL also shows an address-floor hit.

183.text:
The roxy-addon
SDK wraps the bindings for Rust: use roxy_addon::prelude::*;

struct RedactTokens;
impl Layer for RedactTokens {
    fn init(_config: &str) -> Result<Self, String> {   // `config:` as JSON
        Ok(RedactTokens)
    }
    fn handle(&mut self, req: Request, next: Next) -> Response {
        let req = req.map_body(|body| body.transform(redact_chunk));
        next.run(req)
    }
}
roxy_addon::export!(RedactTokens); Body is a pull-based sequence of chunks, read from the host only as the
layer consumes it: transform (per chunk), pipe (a stateful
ChunkTransform that may hold bytes back and flush them at the end) and
read_to_end(cap).Next is consumed by run, so the type system enforces one next per
exchange. next.run returns once the response head arrives, while the
rest of the request body is pumped as the layer reads the response, so a
layer upstream that answers early cannot deadlock against the host's small
body buffers.flow::* and call_endpoint wrap the host services. A panic traps, and
the host fails the exchange closed.WebSockets need nothing extra: the request and response bodies carry
them (WebSockets). Any language that targets the component model works against the WIT. Go
(wasip2) and JS (jco componentize) produce larger binaries with higher
per-call cost. Python in WASM (componentize-py) bundles an interpreter:
tens of MiB, 128–256 MiB of memory, pure-Python dependencies only; give it
raised budgets. Python with native dependencies, or anything else out of
process, is a service layer. roxy-wasm's test component
redact
is a streaming redactor built on roxy-addon.

184.title: Authoring

185.text:
wit/addon.wit
defines the roxy:addon@0.3.0 package.
Heads are records of roxy's own: a
request-head (method, scheme, authority, path and query, and the header
list) and a response-head (status and headers), each crossing the guest
boundary in one call. Bodies are plain wasi:io/streams (vendored at
0.2.12 under wit/deps/; a guest built against any 0.2.x links). The
roxy-addon crate carries its own copy of wit/. World layer exports handler (handle(request-head, input-stream),
one call per exchange) and init (called once per instance, with the
config available through flow.config). It imports types, chain
(next, respond), endpoints, flow, and the WASI clocks, random, io
and stdio interfaces.A layer answers with chain.respond(response-head, body), once, before
handle returns; chain.next(request-head, body) passes a request upstream,
once. Neither waits on the other: a layer may answer and then forward,
forward and answer before the response from upstream arrives, or answer
without forwarding; its answer reaches the client as soon as it is made,
and a forward it made runs on for as long as it waits for the response
(read at least the response head for the forward to be delivered). Both
take a body: empty, bytes (one piece, no stream),
passthrough (a stream the host handed this layer, moved host-side
without entering the guest) or stream, for which the call returns the
output-stream to write. A streamed body must be ended with
types.finish; dropped unfinished it is cut, never ended as complete.next and endpoints.call return a pending-response: subscribe and
get to wait alongside other work, or wait to block and take the
response head and body stream in one call.The host validates every head it is handed: names and values must parse,
there may be no more than limits.max_headers of them, host,
content-length, hop-by-hop and framing fields are refused (roxy derives
them; the body carries its own length), and the whole record must fit in
128 KiB. A refused head fails the exchange closed. Host-side body
passthrough preserves trailers. Guest byte-stream reads and rewrites have
no trailer API, so those paths drop them.The host links the rest of WASI 0.2 inertly: an empty environment, no
arguments, no preopened directories, stdin closed, TCP, UDP and name
lookup off, every socket address denied. Anything a guest writes to
stdout or stderr is discarded; use flow.log to be heard. Stock
toolchains whose standard library imports more than it uses still load,
and still reach nothing.wasi:http is not provided, so a component that imports it fails to
link. Outbound calls go through endpoints.During init there is no exchange: config works, log goes to roxy's
own log (the capability still applies), and every other flow, chain
or endpoints call traps. Build a component against the wit/ of the roxy version it runs on. A
component whose imports do not match fails at config load with the
component's imports named; rebuild it against the current roxy-addon.
185.title: WIT package

186.text:
A component is compiled and linked once per config load, on the blocking
pool, then one instance is started and its init run, so a broken layer
fails the load. Each exchange checks an instance out of the layer's pool
for its whole duration; instances are replaced after
recycle_after_exchanges or above recycle_above_memory, and one that
failed in any way is discarded, never reused
(limits,
configuration).
186.title: Instances

187.text:
An exchange is one request and its response. Every exchange takes the same
path, whichever way roxy is deployed.
187.title: How roxy works

188.text:
A listener accepts the connection. On an http_proxy listener a CONNECT
opens a tunnel; roxy checks that its first bytes are a TLS ClientHello
(by default its SNI, if sent, must name the CONNECT host), terminates TLS
with a leaf from its own CA, and reads HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 inside;
http.allow_plain_in_connect also admits plain HTTP in the tunnel
(CONNECT). On an http listener TLS ends at
the load balancer in front and roxy reads plain origin-form requests
(HTTP). Either way the connection then carries a
sequence of exchanges (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive) or concurrent ones (HTTP/2
streams). roxy parses each request head into one canonical form, which is what it
sends upstream; ambiguous input is rejected, not resolved, so what the
rules and addons see is exactly what is forwarded
(canonical request). The body stays a
stream.
188.title: Decrypt and parse

189.text:
Logic that needs to understand the traffic goes in an addon: an external
service that the traffic streams through, or a WASM component that runs
in process. An addon owns both lanes of the exchanges it chooses and can
rewrite, withhold, answer or block. Requests pass through addons in their
configured order, then reach the core stage. The core validates the final
request, evaluates the rules, applies destination restrictions and owns
the upstream connection. The rules judge the forwarded request as if the
client had sent it
(addon model,
addon configuration).
189.title: Addons

190.text:
The rules are a list of allows plus the denies that restrict them, in one
YAML file. A matching deny always wins, and anything no rule allows is
denied. The forwarding decision is made before the request goes upstream;
rules that read the bodies or the response are re-checked in flight as they
stream, and can still stop the exchange. Metrics give rate limits and byte
budgets (policy evaluation). secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }

rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # the client never sees the key
      - allow

  - id: upload-cap                         # re-checked as the body streams
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and body.bytes > 10mb
    then: { deny: { status: 413 } } The request steps run in a fixed order: a bounded body buffer only when a
rule reads body.text, then the admission decision and its effects. The
lease is checked before the addons run and again
at admission, so a request an addon held across expiry is denied. The only
verdict that leads to the upstream is Continue; every error maps to a
deny or a close. The steps are not an extension point: extensions are
addons, downstream of them.
190.title: Rules

191.text:
The upstream connector resolves the host itself, checks every candidate IP
against the address floor, and connects. A name that resolves somewhere
private is refused, and so is a redirect target or addon endpoint that
does (upstream,
address floor).
191.title: Connect

192.text:
When the response head arrives, the response steps run: a bounded buffer
of the response body only when a rule reads response.body.text, then the
in-flight rules, which may still stop the exchange or change the head. As
body bytes stream roxy re-checks those rules, records byte metrics,
and holds each chunk until the flow log is ready. The response is re-framed
for the client and passes back up the addon stack.
192.title: Respond

193.text:
Every stage writes to the flow log: one JSON line per exchange, naming the
rule that decided, the addons that ran and what changed. The log never
drops a record; when it falls behind, traffic waits
(flow log).
193.title: Log

194.text:
The compiled policy (rules, metrics, addons, address lists) is an immutable
snapshot swapped atomically on reload, and an exchange runs to the end on
the snapshot it started with, except that each lease check uses the
currently loaded policy's expiry. In node mode the
snapshot comes from a control plane's lease instead of a file, and the flow
log is also shipped back to it.
194.title: Policy snapshots

195.text:
roxy knows HTTP, not any particular application or API. Logic that needs to
understand the traffic goes in an addon: a layer downstream of the rules
that owns both lanes of every exchange it runs on. An addon is either: a WASM layer (kind: wasm): a WebAssembly component run in-process by
roxy-wasm, written against the roxy:addon WIT package
(wit/addon.wit),
which hands each head over as one record and each body as a stream; ora service layer (kind: service): an external service in the network
path, which each exchange streams through over a WebSocket
(service layer protocol).
195.title: Addon model

196.text:
An exchange is two lanes. The request lane flows upstream, from the
client through the layers to the rules and the connector; the response
lane flows downstream, from wherever it starts through the same layers to
the client. Each lane is a head, bytes and an end, and the lanes carry no
HTTP rules of their own: what a head or a chunk means is for the two ends
of the proxy, the downstream socket and the upstream connector, to say. A layer sits on both lanes of every exchange it runs on. On either lane it
may pass what it was given, hold it, rewrite it, or originate its own,
chunk by chunk, at any time. roxy infers nothing across the lanes: a
layer's answer on the response lane says nothing about the request lane,
which runs on upstream as the layer drives it. A layer that answers and
wants nothing forwarded forwards nothing; one that answers and forwards
has a forward that runs on for as long as it waits for the response to it.
Each layer must keep its output coherent for the next consumer. The
stack ensures that one valid request reaches the upstream socket and one
valid response reaches the client socket.                  request ↓                                   ↑ response
 fixed   ┌─ CONNECT gate (SNI must match) ───────────────────────────────┐
 config  ├─ addon: first listed                                          │
 config  ├─ addon: second listed                                         │
 fixed   ├─ rules                  (admission ↓ / in flight ↑)           │
 fixed   ├─ address floor + deny lists (on the IP actually dialled)      │
 fixed   └─ connector ──▶ origin ────────────────────────────────────────┘ Addons always sit downstream of the rules, in the order listed under
addons:. A layer with a when runs only on the exchanges it matches
(choosing exchanges).
Nothing configurable runs between the rules and the network, so what the
rules judged is what leaves. The stack is a pipeline: every layer runs at once, as its own task, each
seeing what the downstream layer passed on. On a long stream each works
on a different chunk at the same time. Observe layers get copies and run beside
the stream rather than in it.
196.title: Two lanes

197.text:
Upstream means toward the origin; downstream means toward the client.
The client edge connects the HTTP transport handler to the first pair
of lanes. The core stage is the upstream end of the chain: it validates
the final forwarded request, evaluates admission and in-flight rules,
applies destination restrictions through the connector, and owns upstream
processing through completion, including any WebSocket relay. Addon layers
run between these two stages. Between two neighbouring stages (the client edge, each layer, the core
stage) run two lanes: a request lane, produced by the downstream stage and
consumed by the upstream one, and a response lane the other way. Each lane
is shaped like an HTTP/2 stream. Its producer may put on it at most one
head, then bytes, then trailers once, then either an end (complete) or a
cut (incomplete, with a reason); its consumer may stop it (read no more).
A lane that is ended or cut before any head carries nothing: a headless
request lane is no forward, a headless response lane from a layer is no
answer. A lane that has ended, been cut or been stopped is terminal and
never moves again; what a producer puts on a terminal lane is discarded. The lifecycle rules are: A stage is done when its driver and body workers have finished.
Ending an output lane does not by itself finish the stage: it may still
consume its inputs or run host-service calls. Letting go of an unfinished
input stops that lane.A stop on a request lane tells its producer and nothing else: the
upstream stopped reading the forward, and the layer keeps its other
lanes.A stop on an unfinished response lane tears its producer down: that
stage and every stage upstream of it are cancelled. Unfinished outputs
are cut and held inputs are released. Cancellation reaches stages even
when an intermediate response has already ended. Releasing a completed
response alone does not cancel a still-useful forward.Client cancellation tears down the whole exchange, independently of
which response lanes have ended. HTTP/2 continues watching for stream
resets while waiting for the exchange after an early answer. After a
WebSocket upgrade, socket read and write failures report cancellation
before releasing any lane bodies. A lane-body error alone does not mean
the client disappeared; a clean socket half-close still permits the
other direction to drain.A layer that lets go of its response lane without a head has not
answered: that is its no_response fault.A layer that faults (a trap, a budget, a missed deadline, a lane out
of grammar, a reset, an invalid head attributed to it, or no answer) has its fault recorded before it is cancelled. If its response
lane has no head, roxy puts the corresponding HTTP error response there
for the downstream layers to handle like any other response.A layer answered if the response lane it consumes had no head when
it put its own head on the lane it produces, decided then and never
re-derived. The first fault recorded stands, and a layer's is logged
once.A layer cutting a lane it produces is an abort, not a fault: the
record says forward_aborted or answer_aborted, and the consumer sees
an incomplete body. A headless response cut from an enforcing layer is
still its no_response fault and generates a refusal.A producer's end does not acknowledge delivery. Its queued frames
still belong to the consumer until read or discarded. Trailers are held
until the clean end and length checks succeed, because HTTP trailers
complete the message on the wire. Declared length is a validation
property: an unfinished lane uses unknown-length HTTP/1.1 framing so
even a cut after the declared bytes cannot look complete. HEAD and
bodiless statuses commit at the head; their internal body still runs
under the response idle deadline.The exchange is over when every lane is terminal, its consumers have
finished or abandoned their bodies, and all drivers and enforcing
host-service workers have returned. Upstream upload accounting is final
before its owner returns. Guest drivers and their spawned next, endpoint
and body-finish workers, service pumps and upload monitors belong to this
barrier even when their parent is cancelled. Cancellation includes their
actual destruction, not just an abort request.
Both HTTP transports observe client loss through reclamation. The flow
record is written after this barrier.
WebSockets use the same rule: the core owns the relay and its accounting
until it ends, then cancels any remaining layers. The socket reader and
writer are included in the completion barrier through their destruction. Wire completion, exchange completion and connection lifetime are separate.
An HTTP/1.1 answer can finish while its upload or addon work continues;
reclamation keeps driving the request and any suppressed response body
concurrently. Only after reclamation can that connection serve a pipelined
request, and a late closing refusal still prevents reuse. A full pipeline
buffer has a bounded reclamation deadline. Observers are not stages: an observe layer gets copies of both lanes of a
hop, nothing it produces moves a lane, and the exchange does not wait for
it. A head-only layer puts its head on a lane and the body of the lane it
consumes in the same direction goes on with it (for a response, only when
the status is the same; otherwise the answer is the layer's own, whole).
The bypassed body and the layer's own output have independent ends. Bytes
flow without waiting for the layer's end, but lane completion and trailers
wait for both. This is the same contract for WASM streams and service
request_end / response_end messages, even when no bytes are visible to
the layer or sent on the wire. A head-only service's response end is still
subject to the response idle deadline after a HEAD or 204 answer.
197.title: Lanes, and the rules that move them

198.text:
A layer may answer before forwarding, while forwarding, or without ever
forwarding. A response head does not imply that the request lane has ended.
Responses can originate at any stage: the origin's response through the
connector, a refusal from the rules or address checks, a layer's own
answer, or a 503 generated for a failed layer. Each enters the response
lane at that stage and flows downstream through the layers before it
like any other response: a layer sees the rules' 403 from next as it
would see a 403 from the origin, and may pass it on or replace it with a successful response. Addons are trusted
configuration, so that is theirs to decide; the request did not leave, and
the flow log records the rules' verdict whatever the client was given
(in the proxy). A layer answering without forwarding and the rules refusing are the same
event at different stages: the request lane ends there, that stage
produces the response, and nothing further upstream ever sees the request. A body that stops short upstream of a layer (an in-flight deny cut it, the
origin's body failed) ends that lane with the failure, not the exchange:
the layer sees the lane end short of complete and finishes its own lanes
as it sees fit. Only the client's own request failing ends the exchange
outright, since nothing can answer a client whose request broke.
198.title: Request and response production are independent

199.text:
The lanes are opaque. What reaches a socket is not: the request the last
layer passes upstream is re-validated as strictly as a client's and judged
by the rules, and the response the first layer passes downstream is
re-framed as strictly as an origin's. A head that cannot go out where it
arrives (a second final response head, a 101 that relays no upgrade, a
1xx other than a relayed 101) is the fault of the last layer that
touched it, and becomes a response on the lane downstream of it like any
other failure; a body that does not match the length its head declared is
cut, since its head is already out. Between the two ends a layer may do as
it likes with what it holds, so long as what leaves it is something the
next layer can carry.
199.title: The two ends of the proxy enforce validity

200.text:
Two things come out of a layer, and roxy orders only one of them. The exchange's bytes form a pipeline. A head or a chunk reaches layer B
only after layer A has sent it on, and A may hold, rewrite or drop it on
the way: what B reads is what A passed, in the order A passed it, and the
rules admit the request the last layer forwarded. The response is the same
pipeline in the downstream direction: the rules see the upstream's bytes
first, then B, and A gets a chunk only after B has passed it. This holds
for enforce layers of either kind. An observer is in neither order: it reads a copy
beside the pipeline, holds nothing up, and can neither tag nor write
state, so the rest of this section is about enforce layers. Host-service effects are not in that pipeline. add_tag, state_put,
record and quarantine run independently of the request and response
lanes. Each layer has a worker that runs its calls in order. There is no
implicit ordering between one layer's call and another layer's read:
A's state_put and B's state_get are concurrent unless A awaits its result before sending the bytes B will read. B cannot read on
a chunk it has not received, so the await puts A's write ahead of B's
read. A WASM layer's call is a synchronous function that returns before
the layer continues, so it has that order by construction; a service layer
sends the call as a message and awaits the result itself
(host services on a stream). So, to make an effect visible: to the layers upstream: await the result before sending the head or
chunk whose handling should see it (a WASM layer's call has returned by
the time it sends anything);to this exchange's admission rules: land it before the request is
forwarded, so before the layer calls next or the service sends its
forwarded request head;otherwise, the write is seen by the next rule that reads it. A tag
lives on this exchange, so that is an in-flight re-check of it; state
persists, so it is that or a later exchange's admission. The write does
not itself trigger a re-check: a rule runs when a value it watches
changes, and reads the tag or key then. A write never reopens a decision
already made (policy evaluation).
200.title: Ordering across layers

201.text:
The rules evaluate every request that leaves. An addon can reshape
traffic freely; its output is re-validated by the canonical model and
then judged by the rules exactly as if the client had sent it. On the
way back, the in-flight rules see the upstream's response before any
addon does.Every layer is held to the workload's limits. Whatever a layer passes
on is treated as if a client sent it: header limits, body caps, idle
timeouts. A layer cannot pass on CONNECT: a tunnel is something the
client opens at the proxy port, never a request to forward.Failure is closed. A layer that traps, exceeds a budget or passes on
an invalid head produces a 503 on the lane downstream of it, which the
layers there may reshape but the client gets if none does; after the
response head is out, the body is cut. There is no "on error, pass";
observe mode is the one safe way to run a layer whose failures must not
matter.One forward and one answer per layer. A layer sends the request lane
upstream at most once and the response lane downstream exactly once. In
which order, and how far apart, is its own affair.
201.title: Invariants

202.text:
When an exchange fails, one party is blamed, and the first fault recorded
stands. Every party records its own fault before anything downstream of it
can fail on it: a layer as it fails, before its bodies end; a body where it
enters the stack, before a layer reads it; the transport handler when it
cancels the exchange. So what a layer makes of a body or a next that ended on
someone else's failure is a consequence, never a second fault. Final reason selection happens after reclamation, from the facts gathered
by the adapters. A policy or validation reason already in the record is
preserved. Otherwise a known fault behind a failed response body takes
precedence, followed by a deliberate lane abort, observed cancellation,
a response failure, an upload deadline, and finally upstream abandonment.
Writing and discarding a response body use the same fault attribution.
A later drain failure does not turn an already-written HEAD or bodiless
response into a failed wire write, and discarded bytes are not counted as
transmitted. A fault recovered by a layer does not by itself fail a
successfully completed response. A layer's own failure (a trap, an exceeded budget, an invalid head, a
service that broke its stream) is the layer's: 503 with
terminal_rule: layer:<name> before the response head, a cut body after
it, and one layer_error event either way. The 503 travels downstream
on the response lane, so a layer there may reshape what the client gets;
the record is the refusal's either way. A failure found upstream of the
layer that caused it (a passed-on request that does not validate, say) is
put down to the nearest enforcing layer downstream of it.A client upload that breaks is the client's, as without a stack: the
connection closes on the parse error before the head, the body is cut
after it, and no layer_error is logged however many layers fail on the
cut body.An upstream response body that fails before any layer has answered with
a head of its own is the upstream's: 502, reason: upstream_body_failed.
One that fails after that ends the response lane upstream of the layer
with the failure; what the client's response makes of it is the layer's.A body the buffer budget cannot cover on its
way to a layer (a decoder's window) fails closed as the budget's:
reason: buffer_budget_exhausted.An observer is never blamed, and a client that gives up is nobody's
failure: nothing is logged.
202.title: Who is blamed

203.text:
A layer calls next at most once per exchange; a second call traps. The
stack carries the client's traffic and nothing else: a layer never
originates requests through the layers upstream of it, so retrying, regenerating
or replaying is the client's job, and a layer that rejects something
answers with a response the client can act on. Anything else a layer needs
to reach is a named endpoint,
which goes straight to the connector, never through other layers or the
rules. next and the layer's answer are the two lanes, and neither waits on the
other. A layer may answer first and forward after, forward and answer
before the response from upstream arrives, or answer and never forward.
Its answer reaches the client as soon as it is made. A forward is carried
upstream only while something downstream waits for its response: a layer
that wants its forward delivered reads at least the response head. A layer
that stops reading the response (drops the pending response, or returns
without reading it) has the upstream request cancelled; the forward's body
is still the layer's to finish or cut. A layer that cuts a lane of its own
(drops a body unfinished) has aborted it: nothing comes back for a cut
forward, and the record says forward_aborted or answer_aborted; that
is not a failure. A layer that fails is torn down, and everything upstream
of it with it. Once a layer is done with the client's upload, the rest of
it is dropped rather than held for a reader that will never come.
203.title: One exchange, one next

204.text:
A layer subscribes to each direction in config: the head and the body
(full, the default) or the head only. Of a direction it has in full, a
layer may read, rewrite, split, delay, inject into or replace the stream,
chunk by chunk. roxy buffers nothing on a layer's behalf; a layer that
wants a whole body reads it, within its max_memory. The patterns:
observe (next(req), return its response unchanged), rewrite in flight
(wrap a body stream in a transform), withhold until cleared (forward a
streamed response as it arrives but hold back parts, say tool calls, until
judged), and deny or answer (return a response without calling next). A body a layer is not subscribed to bypasses it, as if the layer had
passed it on untouched: the layer sees the head with an empty body and
decides at admission, and roxy splices the body onto what it passes on. An
enforce layer still denies or rewrites at admission; an observer that wants
heads only costs no body copies
(what a layer sees). A WebSocket is an exchange like any other, only long-lived: after the
101, the request body carries the client's bytes and the response body
the upstream's (WebSockets through addons).
Layers see bodies decoded, so none needs its own decompressors
(content codings).
204.title: A layer takes what it subscribes to

205.text:
mode: enforce (default): the layer is in the path and its decisions
take effect.mode: observe: roxy tees both lanes to the layer and ignores
anything it returns except host-service calls such as record. The
layer cannot change or delay traffic, so its failures cannot weaken
containment: a trap or missed deadline is logged, not fatal, which makes
it the way to deploy an uncalibrated monitor. sample gives it a share
of the matching exchanges, and an observer may record but cannot tag
the flow (capabilities).Each copy of a body the layer is subscribed to is buffered for it, so
one that keeps up sees every body in full, however large. A copy is cut, and the flow goes on, when
the layer falls limits.max_observer_lag_bytes behind, the
buffer budget cannot cover its next frame,
or no instance of the layer comes free within its first_byte_timeout
(observer_lagged, with the reason). A request refused or answered
upstream of the observer without its body being read ends the copy
where reading stopped, without an error, and the observer sees the refusal
from next; a copy that fails (the client went away mid-upload) ends
with that failure, so the layer can tell the two apart.
205.title: Modes

206.text:
On ordinary HTTP traffic roxy is on a par with Envoy. As a gateway it
handles about 30% more small requests per core, with a lower median latency
at both light and heavy concurrency, and moves the same bytes per second on
large bodies for about a quarter more CPU
(#104). As an egress
proxy it is ahead at every size, by a third to a half per core. Doing TLS
interception it handles about 20 times the small requests per core of
mitmproxy, falling to about 3 times on 1 MiB bodies, with a median latency
in milliseconds rather than hundreds of milliseconds. requests per core, roxy relative to1 KiB64 KiB1 MiBEnvoy, as a gateway1.3x1.0x0.8xEnvoy, as an egress proxy1.5x1.3x1.3xmitmproxy, doing TLS interception19x8x2.7x
206.title: Performance

207.text:
An addon is a fixed charge on the throughput roxy would otherwise have,
before the addon's own work, and a charge per byte on the bodies that
stream through it. A WASM layer that forwards
everything unchanged costs about half of the small-request throughput and
most of it on large bodies; a service layer
doing the same costs about 60% on small requests and most of it on large
bodies, plus whatever the sidecar and its network hop add. Most of the
body cost is common to both kinds and is paid even when the layer leaves
the body untouched: it is in the lane pipeline between the stages
(#558), with the
service's socket on top. throughput lost to a do-nothing layer, as an egress proxy1 KiB64 KiB1 MiBWASM layerabout 50%about 70%about 85%service layer (sidecar on localhost)about 60%about 75%about 90% In CPU terms, roxy spends about 100 µs on a small exchange with no addons
and a do-nothing layer of either kind adds roughly another 100 µs: the calls
into the host for WASM, a dozen messages over a second socket for a service.
So a layer that does T µs of work per request makes an exchange cost about
200 + T µs, and four cores give roughly 4,000,000 / (200 + T) requests per
second: 20,000 with no work, 13,000 at 100 µs, 4,000 at 800 µs. A service
layer adds the sidecar's own CPU on top. A body through a layer adds about
3 µs per KiB for WASM and 4.5 µs per KiB for a service, so a 1 MiB response
through a do-nothing layer costs roxy 4 to 5 ms against about 0.6 ms with
no addons.
207.title: What an addon costs

208.text:
No run uses body rules,
capture, body digests or a real addon. A
digest costs about one core per 400 MB/s on a CPU without SHA-NI, which is
why it is opt-in. These figures come from one machine, measured against Envoy and mitmproxy
and with a do-nothing addon of each kind; the detail on the fixed cost is
in #403 and
#425. The addon
rows were re-taken after the lane pipeline
(#558); the Envoy and
mitmproxy rows were not.
208.title: What is not measured

209.text:
The policy decides what roxy forwards, what it denies, and what it changes
on the way. It is a list of rules in the config file, each with an id, a
when condition in the rule language and a
then with one or more actions.
Anything no rule allows is denied: rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: no-admin-paths
    when: path starts_with "/admin"
    then: deny
209.title: Policy evaluation

210.text:
An exchange is a set of values that become known over time: the request
head, request body bytes as they stream, the response head, response body
bytes, and the metric values this exchange adds to. Rules are one ordered
list of conditions over those values. There are no phases: when a rule
runs follows from what it reads. A request is judged at two points. Each layer's when is checked on the
head as it arrives; the rules decide the head once, after the whole stack
and before anything is forwarded (if a rule reads body.text, the body is
buffered up to the cap first: body rules),
then re-check the body as its bytes stream past. When a layer's tag or
state write becomes visible to the rules, and to the layers upstream of it, is a
matter of ordering across layers. The forwarding decision is made at the request head, and deny wins.
roxy evaluates every rule whose values are known at that point. If any
matching rule denies, the request is denied; otherwise, if any matching
rule allows, it is allowed; otherwise it is denied with rule id
_default, so an empty rule set denies everything. To let traffic
through while you find out what a workload reaches, say so with a rule:
{ id: discover, then: allow } (no when matches everything). Rule order does
not affect the decision. A rule that reads a value not yet known is
skipped here, not treated as false. quarantine is a deny that also
puts the proxy into quarantine: a
matching one trips it whichever deny decided the request, a fail-closed
included, and from the next exchange on nothing here runs at all.After that, rules run in flight. For the rest of the exchange, two
kinds of rule are re-checked whenever a value they read becomes known or
changes: rules that read an in-flight field
(fields), and deny or quarantine
rules that read a byte metric (count: request_bytes or
response_bytes), which this exchange adds to as bytes stream. A deny
reading a requests, denied, errors or unique metric is decided at
admission only: re-checking it after this exchange's own count would deny
the 30th request of a >= 30 limit instead of the 31st. body.bytes is
first checked when the request body's first bytes arrive, so a rule that
reads only it never fires for an empty body; response.body.bytes is
checked at the response head, where it is 0, and again as the body
streams. If an in-flight deny matches, roxy stops the
exchange: an error response if the response has not started, otherwise
HTTP/1.1 breaks the connection without finishing the body and HTTP/2
resets the stream. Nothing overrides a deny.Only admission rules can allow. A rule that reads an in-flight
field cannot allow, change the request (set_header on the request,
rewrite_path, redirect, ...), capture or digest: the request is
already on its way, so each is a compile error. It can deny or
quarantine, and add effects that still make sense: log, tag,
set_state, and header changes on a response that has not been sent
yet.An in-flight rule's non-terminal effects apply once, the first time it
matches.Order matters for effects, not decisions. Rules are evaluated top to
bottom. If the request is allowed, the effects of every matching rule
apply in list order; if two set the same header, the later wins. A deny
does not cut evaluation short, at admission or in flight: every
rule the pass checks still runs. If the request is denied, or a change
to it fails (which denies it with _fail_closed, reason
effect_invalid), the log and set_state effects of the matching
rules still apply, and the request's metric samples count it as denied.
An unavailable input is the exception: it stops admission evaluation at that
rule, so the rules below it do not run, their log and set_state do
not apply, and rules in the flow log lists only the rules above it.
Allow options (upgrade, private_ok) come from the first matching
allow only. The flow log names the first matching deny (or allow) as
terminal_rule.A tag is visible to the rules below the rule that set it. A rule
that reads a tag must come after every rule that sets it (an admission
rule above it, or, for an in-flight rule, any admission rule); otherwise
the config is rejected, since moving a rule would change what it sees. A
tag set by an in-flight rule can be read by no other rule: in-flight
rules fire when the values they read arrive, not in list order, so
whether the tag was visible would depend on timing. A deny or
quarantine that reads a byte metric can fire in flight too, so an
in-flight rule cannot read its tag; an admission rule below it can. A
rule may read its own tag, and a
tag no rule sets (from an addon). roxy check and roxy rule test report whether each rule is decided at
admission or in flight. Unavailable inputs fail closed. If a rule needs a metric value, an
address-list lookup or a secret and it is unavailable (store overloaded,
table full, list failed to load), the flow is denied with 503,
terminal_rule: _fail_closed, and a policy_input_unavailable event. So
is a field whose value is not of its documented type (reason wrong_type):
that is a bug in roxy, and a predicate over it has no answer. A field that
is simply absent, like an unsent header, is not unavailable: it is null
(missing values).
210.title: Evaluation

211.text:
roxy is a security boundary for the HTTP traffic that reaches it. These
guarantees decide every behaviour on the other pages; where a page says
"fails closed" or "deny wins", this is why.
211.title: Threat model and guarantees

212.text:
Attacker: the client. It controls every byte it sends to roxy, may run
arbitrary code, and may have root inside its own container or VM. Trusted: the host, roxy's binary and config, the secrets roxy holds, the
public CA trust store used to verify upstreams, the upstreams the rules
allow, and the proxies a listener's forwarded_for counts: the trusted
hops of X-Forwarded-For are taken as written, so a client's identity is
only as good as the load balancer that appended it, and the network must
let only those proxies reach the listener. A hop that is missing or is not
an address refuses the request rather than falling back to the peer
(HTTP). Upstream responses are not treated as adversarial; roxy applies the
size and time limits that protect its own resources and re-frames them so
the client sees one clean wire form. For traffic that reaches it, in a sandbox and a
gateway alike, roxy prevents: reaching any destination the rules do not allow, including through
Host/SNI spoofing, DNS rebinding, redirects to private ranges, CONNECT to
arbitrary ports, or non-HTTP protocols tunnelled through CONNECT;desync and smuggling between roxy and the upstream, or between roxy and
the client, through ambiguous framing;exfiltrating real credentials: with secret injection the client only ever
holds placeholders;unbounded memory and file-descriptor use from slowloris, huge headers,
unbounded bodies and cardinality attacks, within the configured limits;learning anything useful from a deny beyond the rule id. roxy does not try to prevent traffic that never reaches it, timing or
DNS side channels from the workload (block DNS egress at the network layer;
roxy resolves names itself), compromise of an upstream the rules already
allow, or compromise of the host running roxy. WASM addons have memory,
instance and answer-deadline limits. Epoch yielding makes guest code
cancellable and shares execution time; it is not a total CPU budget. A
handler that has answered can continue consuming CPU until its exchange is
cancelled, so addon configuration remains trusted.
212.title: Threat model

213.text:
roxy is not a transparent proxy: it decides what passes through it and
cannot stop traffic that never reaches it. Sandbox containment claims that all of the workload's traffic goes
through roxy. That claim is the network's: the workload must have no
route out except roxy's proxy port, with direct TCP, UDP and DNS blocked
at the boundary (sandbox containment). The proxy
variables and the CA only tell a well-behaved client where roxy is.An HTTP gateway makes no such claim. It governs the requests its
clients send to it; the clients keep whatever other routes they have
(HTTP gateway). roxy speaks HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and WebSockets to clients. Raw TCP does not
pass.
213.title: Which use case claims what

214.text:
In node mode the node is a bearer token the control
plane issued at enrolment, kept in the state dir (mode 0600) and
presented inside the server's TLS on every request. What it protects
against is a host that was never enrolled, or one the operator has cut
off: the control plane accepts leases, flow batches and renewals only
from tokens it issued, each token expires and is renewed, and revocation
(410) is per node and immediate. The node never re-enrols on its own,
so a lost token is a stopped node, not a new one. It does not protect against the host roxy runs on: whatever can read the
state dir holds the node's identity, as it would hold any credential kept
there, and the host is already trusted. Nor does it bind the token to a
connection; a token read from the node can be replayed from elsewhere
until it expires or the node is revoked, which is why the control plane
should store tokens hashed and keep their lifetime short.
214.title: Node identity

215.text:
Anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is dropped. An empty rule
set denies everything, and so does a policy past its valid_until
(lease). A config that fails to compile is not
loaded, and a failed reload keeps the running policy. An addon in
enforce mode that fails denies the flow; an observe addon cannot
affect traffic, so its failure is logged and the flow goes on. An
unavailable policy input denies the flow rather than making a predicate
false. A quarantine, once tripped, denies
everything across reloads and restarts until lifted from outside the
process. Resource limits lists
every case.
215.title: Fail closed

216.text:
Requests are parsed into a strict internal model and re-emitted in one
unambiguous wire form; nothing the client sends reaches the upstream
byte-for-byte. Ambiguous input is rejected rather than resolved, and what
the rules match is exactly what is forwarded (HTTP).
After a WebSocket upgrade the connection carries only that WebSocket;
when a rule reads messages, each is decoded strictly and re-encoded in one
form (WebSockets).
216.title: Canonical re-serialisation

217.text:
Any matching deny wins over any matching allow, wherever it sits in the
list, and nothing overrides a deny later in an exchange. Rule order orders
effects, never decisions, so adding a deny can only narrow what passes
(policy evaluation).
217.title: Deny always wins

218.text:
Bounded tables (metric series, the state store) never evict to make
room. A flow that needs a new entry in a full table is denied instead, so a
client cannot reset its own counter by churning keys
(rate limits).
218.title: Never evict

219.text:
The flow log and traffic capture never drop a record. When a log falls
behind or its disk fails, roxy holds traffic back until it catches up
(flow log).
219.title: Audit backpressure

220.text:
Addons sit downstream of the rules and can reshape traffic freely, but what they
pass on is re-validated as strictly as a client request and judged by the
rules as if the client had sent it. Nothing configurable runs between the
rules and the network, and the address floor checks the IP actually
dialled. A refusal the rules make travels downstream through the addons as a
response. A downstream addon may reshape it, including into a success
response: addons are trusted configuration, the request did not leave, and the flow log records the rules' verdict whatever the client was
given (addon model).
220.title: The rules judge everything that leaves

221.text:
An exchange is a request head, a request body stream, a response head and a
response body stream. A body is buffered only when a rule or addon needs
its content, up to a cap, and the buffers of all exchanges together stay
within one process-wide budget (limits). Memory
use grows with neither body size nor the number of clients holding a
buffer.
221.title: Streams, not messages

222.text:
Strictness is aimed at malformed or ambiguous traffic. A conforming
HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 client doing ordinary things (large uploads, keep-alive,
100-continue, WebSockets, redirects, compression) through an allowed rule
should notice nothing except the CA. A default that trips a conforming
client is a bug.
222.title: Well-behaved clients work unhindered
